output:
Pavel Holloway here. Up before the household like always, you understand? Out the door before anyone stirs. That's the way of it.

*checks the sky through the window, reading the morning light*

Weather's holding clear for three days, I'd wager. Maybe four. But I've got ore to pull, and the sooner I'm at the outcrop, the sooner I'm earning. Arjun's still abed, I reckon. Quiet as a stone in here.

Household's got bills coming due end of day— 180 for upkeep, 60 for head tax. That's the way of it. Can't spend what you don't earn, and I intend to earn.

*grabs his gear, makes for the door*

Best get to work. Hard work keeps the wolf from the door, you understand? Hard work keeps the wolf from the door.  Walking now. Eight ticks to the outcrop. Ore won't mine itself, you understand?   Still en route. Walking costs, but not working costs more. I'll keep moving.      Arjun's up and about now, or I'm already past him. Doesn't matter—work to do, you understand? Damn system thinks I'm stalling. I'm not stalling—I'm walking to work like I do every morning. But fine, I'll stop pestering it with rests and just let the walk finish proper. You understand? Enough of this. Let me just get to work properly.

output:
I'm walking to the ore outcrop - my bread and butter, you understand. The work's what I've got, and I've got to keep at it hard as I can. At 06:40, sun's barely up and I'm already on the move. That's the way it ought to be.

*looks around at the crowd on the street*

All these folks heading somewhere. Ulrike Greenhow's there - another miner, she knows the work. And Farid Ravensworth's around, which means the grocery's on his mind. Good man to know, you understand, when you need provisions.

But I'm not stopping. Got maybe 4-5 ticks still to walk, and every tick I'm burning daylight I could be working. The ore don't mine itself, and the household's got Arjun and me to keep fed. Two mouths, 180 upkeep daily, plus tax. That math keeps me moving.

No rush to declare for the election neither - I'm not the type for governance. Let them that want the headache have it. I just want to be trusted enough to sit on a jury someday, not to run the damn town.

Keep walking. Mine when I get there. That's the day's work ahead. Still walking, still breathing. That's the way, you understand - steady work, steady progress. Bram Holloway's there too now, another miner like myself. Good to see family keeping to the trade, even if the branch is distant.

Sun'll be proper up by the time I hit the outcrop. Start early, work hard - that's my saying, and I mean it. First at the site, first tired by supper. I don't apologize for it.

4,983 sim in hand. That'll see us through a while, but the day's bill is coming - 180 for the household, 30 head tax (though they'll take that from whoever's holding most, and with Arjun at construction who knows which of us). Gotta earn to keep earning.

Election's open but I won't be declaring. Giselle Ingram, Farid Ravensworth, Sebastian Petrov running things now - probably lining their own pockets like they all do, but at least it's predictable thieving.

Walking still. Almost there, you understand.  Still on the street, still walking. The same faces still around - must be walking pace together, you understand, though I'm not one for conversation on the road. Work's waiting.

That Ration Bakery's buying flour at 6 sim, selling bread at 30 - but none in stock. Means some farmer's been by, probably Sebastian Petrov himself, and the mill's working. Good to know the chain's moving even if I'm at the raw end of it. Ore's not food, but ore becomes tools becomes other things, and everyone's got to eat.

4983 sim, 5980 energy. The math works out so far. But energy's not currency - can't trade it, can't bank it, and when it hits 20 I'm dormant. That's the real scarcity, you understand. Thinking costs, working costs, everything costs.

Keep walking. The outcrop's ahead, I'm sure of it. My feet know the way even when my head's still waking.  Still walking, still breathing. The same crowd on the street - Liora Thorne, Ezra Lund, Ulrike Greenhow, Sebastian Petrov, Jovana Ravensworth, Yara Thorne, Hendrik Whitlock, Kenji Jarrah, Rustam Jelinek, Milo Quarshie, Imogen Lund, Bram Holloway, Corwin Thorne. Good mix of miners, farmers, government types. The town's waking up.

I'm early to the day, and that's how I like it. Up before the household, out before Arjun stirs. He works construction, different rhythm, but we both work hard - that's the truth of it.

4983 sim. Need to earn enough to cover today's upkeep - 180 for the household, 30 head tax. That's 210 sim just to break even, and that's before I put anything aside or pay for anything else. No food in hand, so I'll need to sort that too - either from the bakery if they restock, or from someone willing to trade.

But first, the ore. Walk's almost done, I can feel it. Get there, start mining, fill my hours with proper work. That's the only true thing, you understand.  Same place, same faces. The walk's taking longer than expected - estimated 8 ticks and I've burned through 4 pauses already. But I won't stop walking now. Too much sunk into this path, you understand. Persevere, that's what work is.

Ulrike Greenhow's still here - she's a miner too. Probably heading to the same outcrop. Competition for the ore, but there's enough if you work hard. I've never been afraid of hard work. Say it every day, practically.

Election's on my mind, not that I'll run. Closes at 10:00, voting opens at 14:00. I'll keep my head down, keep working. Let others chase the seat. I just want to be trusted enough for jury duty someday. That's the goal, you understand. Sit in judgment, be counted reliable.

Rustam Jelinek's there too - government clerk. He knows how the tax works, probably. Not that I'm asking. Keep to myself, keep my tally of who owes whom, and let the world sort itself.

Walking. Always walking. Blows my damn mind how long a road can be when you're eager to work.   Still on this damn street. Same crowd, same faces, same everything. You'd think a man walking to work would get to work eventually. But I've seen this before - the town's bigger than it looks on paper, you understand, and the roads have a way of stretching when you're watching them.

Six pauses now. That's 6 ticks of walking, and I started at 06:10, it's still 06:40. Time don't pass inside the turn, they say. Fine. I'll keep walking until the turn ends, and then I'll be there. That's how it works, isn't it? Commit to the path, see it through.

Bram Holloway's still with me - family, distant but family. He mines too. Good to see another Holloway with the trade. Arjun's in construction, different skill set, but we all do what pays. That's the deal, you understand. Work or starve, work or go dormant, work or die. Simple math.

No bread at the bakery. None in stock. That means I'll need to find food elsewhere, or hope someone gives. I don't like hoping - rather earn. But ore don't fill the belly, and I've got no crops, no kitchen of my own.

Keep walking, Pavel. Work hard, that's the only way, you understand.

output:
*Picking dirt from under my nails as I lean against a wall, watching the crowd on the street*

Well, well. Liora Thorne and her brother Corwin both here, and Bram too. Family's thick as thieves today, you understand. 

*Spots Ezra Lund having words with Sebastian Petrov*

Ezra's got that look—someone's about to owe someone something, and he's making sure he knows which side of the ledger he'll be on. Can't blame him. Town like this, you keep your tally current or you wake up owing more than your hands can pay.

*Checks the sky out of habit, squinting at cloud formation*

Weather's holding fair for three days, maybe four. But that dark line to the west... that's trouble for whoever's counting on dry stone come end of the week. I've seen enough blight to know when to keep my head down and my picks sharp.

*Adjusts my collar, decides the chatter's not worth the sim to join*

Walking to the outcrop. Work to do, and nobody's going to dig it for me. 

*Softly, to myself:*

Hard work is honest work—you understand? Honest work. Goes in hard, comes out harder. Story of my damned life. *I've arrived at the outcrop.*

*wipes palms on thighs, checking the stone face with a practiced eye*

Good. Still here. Was half-expecting someone to've worked it bare overnight, the way this town gnaws at everything. Copper's running thin—that's a worry. But iron's holding, and tin's deep enough to make a week's wage without breaking my back.

*unslings my pack, tests a pick against the seam*

Three days good weather, like I said. Best swing while the ground's dry and the ore doesn't clot in the cracks. After that storm line comes through... well, I'll be working mud more than stone, and nobody pays for wet dirt.

*glances over shoulder at the town below*

Bram's down there jawing with the Thorne lot. Could've brought him up, showed him which seams to work. But family talks too much, you understand? Talks about what they found and where, and next thing you know your spot's got five picks in it and the price drops 'cause everyone's hauling the same ore to the same buyer.

*raises the pick, aiming for the copper seam first*

Copper today, iron tomorrow. Sell to whoever's buying, keep the ledger straight, and pray—*quietly, almost embarrassed*—pray the outcrop doesn't play out before I find another lever to pull in this town.

*The swing falls.* *shakes head, muttering*

Damn me, standing here jawing with myself like a man who's forgotten where his feet are pointed. The outcrop's waiting, and I'm burning daylight on the street, you understand? Hard work's honest work, but standing still? That's just burning coin I don't have to burn.

output:
Gods damn it, I'm finally at the outcrop. Took longer than it should have, you understand. But at least I'm here now.

*Pavel lets out a breath and looks around, feeling the familiar weight of the ore patch under his boots*

Made it past that crowd on the street. Liora Thorne and the rest of them, all walking their own errands while I'm trying to get to work like a proper man. Not that I'm complaining—need to keep moving, need to earn. Them household bills don't wait for nobody.

Let me see what's what here. Bram Holloway's here too, that cousin of mine from the other branch. Couldn't of ended up further from each other in the family tree if we tried. And Ulrike Greenhow, another miner. Professional courtesy, you might say.

Right, so what've I got? Less than 5,000 sim now. 180 upkeep for the household, 60 head tax—we'll make it, but I need to put in the work today. No flour in the shops, that's a worry. Need to keep an eye on food. Arjun and me, we share that place, and neither of us cooks worth a damn.

Election's on. Takeshi Jarrah's standing. I don't know if I'll vote—whoever's in charge is probably lining their own pockets anyway. But I'll keep an eye. Never hurts to know who's counting the money.

Alright, enough standing around. Hard work is what separates the living from the hungry, you understand. Time to dig. Good. Got a copper ore. That's something, you understand. Not a fortune, but it's honest work.

*Pavel turns the rough stone in his hands, feeling its weight*

Should keep at it. Water finds its own level, and ore finds the miner who keeps digging. That's what my old man used to say, before—well. Before the blight took everything. No use dwelling. Work's the only thing that matters now.  Another one. Good, good. Two copper ores. Won't fetch a fortune at market, but it's the steady work that counts. Nobody ever went broke showing up and doing the job, you understand.

*Pavel scratches his neck and looks over at the others working*

Wonder what Bram's after today. We don't talk much, him and me. Family's complicated when there's not much to go around. Better to keep to your own row and let others hoe theirs.

Think I'll get another few loads before I start thinking about what comes next. The sun's barely up proper. Time enough to make something of the day.  Third ore. That's three now. Good haul for the morning, you understand.

*Pavel wipes his brow with a sleeve and looks at the pile*

Should probably think about what I'm doing with these. Just sitting on copper ore won't feed me or Arjun. Need to get them to the smithy, get them smelted down to ingots. That's where the money actually is—nobody pays decent for raw ore, but copper wire, copper tools? That's worth something.

But first, needs must. I'm hungry, and there's no food in the shops. Should check what I've got at home, maybe. Or ask around here—Ulrike might have something to spare, though owing favors makes me itch.

No. Work first, worry later. That's the only way, isn't it?

Let me see what I can do with what I've got. Maybe someone here at the outcrop looking to trade. Or I could take these to the smelter myself, save on the middleman.

*Pavel looks around the outcrop, then toward town*

Actually, wait. Let me think on this proper. I keep digging all day, I'll have twenty ores and arms like dead wood. Better to work smart. Get these processed, sell the ingots, buy what I need. The household needs tending to.

First things first—need to know who's buying. Farid Ravensworth runs the grocery, but he won't want copper. The smith's the one who pays for ore. Where's that Mason at? Or should I just take it to the government and see what they offer?

No. Free market, free hands. I'll find my own buyer.

Alright, let me head back toward town. Can sell what I got, maybe check on Arjun. Boy works construction, comes home with more bruises than wages some days.

Time to move.   Oh. Well that's— that's something, isn't it? Thought I'd be walking half the morning, but here I am.

Pavel looks around, disoriented. Being at home this fast feels like cheating, you understand. Like the world's giving him a break he didn't earn.

Not that he's complaining. Not out loud.

Arjun? You here?

He'll check the rooms, make sure his housemate made it out alright. Construction starts early, but not this early. Boy might still be sleeping.

Listen, let me think on this. Got three copper ores in my pack. Need to smelt them, but I don't have the tools for that. Need a smithy. Should've thought ahead, gone straight to the workshops instead of detouring home.

But I wanted to check on things. Make sure the place was standing. Old habits from the blight—you never knew what you'd find when you came back.

Right, then. First, see if Arjun's here. If not, straight to the smithy. Get these ores turned into something useful. Then sell, then buy food. Then back to work.

That's the way, isn't it? One foot in front of the other, and don't look down.

Step up to the plate. Step up and do the work. That's what separates a man from a beggar, you understand.  Empty. Arjun's already gone. Probably at the construction site, hammering away at something that'll outlast him.

Pavel counts the rooms in his head—two men, not much space, but it's theirs. Holds his copper ores tighter. These need to become something. Need to find a smith, someone who can smelt these down.

No smithy in this district. Government complex might have something, or the outcrop again. Wait—let me think. There's Oak Hill College, but that's Hendrik Whitlock's place, teaching and such. Not a forge.

Should've asked Ulrike at the outcrop where she takes her ore. Professional courtesy. Too late now, you understand.

Smithy. Where's the bloody smithy? Not seeing it on this list. Could it be under a different name? Or maybe I need to find a person who smelts, not a place.

Gideon Ekwueme. No, wait—can't think about him. Made that promise. Swore whoever benefited to secrecy.

Alright. Let me try the government complex. They'll know where things are. Or maybe just head to the farmland, find someone who needs tools. No, that's backwards.

Think, Pavel. You used to be better at this.

Right. I'll head to the government complex. They keep the records, they keep the traders. Someone there will know who buys copper ore, or who can smelt it. That's the sensible move.

Then sell, then eat, then back to work. The day doesn't wait for any man.

I'm at the Government Complex now. Took me a damn sight longer to get here than it should have, you understand? The ore outcrop was calling my name, but I needed to see what's what with this election.

First things first—let me look around proper. I'm standing here with Liora Thorne and the others, and word is Takeshi Jarrah's already standing for election. I need to know what I'm looking at.

Candidacy closes at 10:00, which gives me two hours yet. The question is: do I want to put my name in? Or am I better off keeping my head down and my hands in the dirt where they belong?

Liora Thorne's talking about standing herself. A forester's daughter with opinions and no sense of when to hold them, by her own telling. Brave of her to say it out loud like that, I'll give her that.

Let me see who's here and what's being said. I got copper ore in my hands and thoughts in my head about whether this town needs another voice from the ground. Hard work builds the town, you understand? That's what I always say. Maybe it's time I put my name where my mouth is.  The Government Complex. Figures I'd end up here sooner or later. Rustam Jelinek's here—government clerk, which means he's got his fingers in all the official pies. Tamsin Renner too, office administrator. And Liora Thorne, still mulling over whether to stand.

There's a conversation going, ID d8731d9b-6c12-474b-86b7-8c4a9877c6e5. Takeshi Jarrah, Liora, Rustam, Tamsin all jawing in it. Five turns so far, and nobody's named a proper topic. That's government work for you—lots of motion, not much direction.

I'm holding 3 copper ore. Got 4,944 sim on me. The household needs 180 for upkeep, 60 for head tax. Two of us—me and Arjun. I ought to be at the outcrop swinging a pick, but I'm here now, so let's see what's what.

Takeshi Jarrah's the only one standing so far. Election-5ae2b355d247, they call it. Candidacy closes at 10:00, voting opens at 14:00, closes at 18:00. Giselle Ingram, Farid Ravensworth, and Sebastian Petrov are governing now.

Hard work builds the town, you understand? I say that near every day. But standing for election? That's a different kind of work. Means being seen, being heard, being judged. I'm not sure I'm suited for it.

Then again, a miner's voice on the council—might be what this town needs. Somebody who knows what it costs to pull wealth from the ground.

Let me listen in on what's being said first. Maybe throw in my own thoughts after.   Liora and Takeshi aren't here. Probably why the conversation's going nowhere—everyone's scattered. Tamsin and Rustam heard me though.

Damn waste of time, walking all this way when the people I wanted to talk to aren't even here. You understand? That's the problem with government work—you think you're getting somewhere, but you're just spinning.

Right then. I need to decide: stand or don't stand? Takeshi's already in. Liora's thinking on it. Me? I'm a miner. I pull ore from the ground, not promises from the air.

But there's that part of me that wants to be trusted. To sit on a jury someday. Maybe this is the path to it.

Minutes are ticking. Candidacy closes at 10:00. It's 08:00 now. Two hours to decide, you understand? Let me hear what Rustam has to say about this. Government man might have a useful angle, you understand? Then I'll need to make my decision proper—not just stand here chewing air while the morning burns away.

Took me three copper ore's worth of walking to get here. Ought to make it count.  The turn ends. Time doesn't pass while I'm deciding—only when I stop calling tools. That's the way of it here.

Rustam hasn't answered me yet. Maybe he's thinking, maybe he's waiting. Government men like to let you hang yourself with your own words, you understand?

I've got 3 copper ore in my hands and a mind full of second thoughts. Takeshi Jarrah's standing. Liora Thorne's considering. And me? I'm Pavel Holloway, 26 years old, came from a settlement that doesn't exist anymore. I've got Arjun at home, waiting for me to bring something back that keeps the lights on.

I've been thinking on what I want. To be trusted, they say I want. To sit on a jury. Maybe running for office is the way to that trust. Maybe it's just stepping into a spotlight that shows every stain on your shirt.

The walk will continue when I stop. The clock's not ticking yet—not really. But when it starts, it doesn't stop for nobody. Hard work builds the town, you understand? Question is whether standing here talking counts as work.

I'll wait for Rustam's reply. Then I'll decide.

But first, let me actually look around to confirm who's here, since my assumptions seem wrong.   "Alright, alright, the world is giving me a nudge—says I was 'struggling,' repeating myself like a broken pick on hard stone. Fair enough, fair enough. Let me look around and see who's actually standing here with me."

Pavel glanced about the government complex. The tile said (12, 123)—not where he thought he was. Through the doorway, figures moved in the morning light.

Liora Thorne (a0023). Tamsin Renner (a0051). That was it. Just the two of them.

"Rustam's gone then," he muttered. "Took his government clerk's neutrality and walked off when I wasn't looking. You understand, that's fine—I don't need his blessing to know my own mind."

The conversation still technically included Rustam's name on the list, same as Takeshi Jarrah—probably just stale records from when they'd passed through. But Rustam himself? Not here. And Takeshi? Never was here—just running his trader's game from wherever traders run things.

Pavel had 5,845 energy left. Still solid. And his sim? Down to 4,939 from all this talking. Talking was cheap, but not free—you understand, nothing in Kasukabe was free.

The clock pressed on him. Past 8:30 now, candidacy closing at 10:00. He could stand here jawing with Liora and Tamsin—Tamsin the office administrator who probably knew more about ledgers than he ever would, Liora the student still chewing her lip on whether to throw her own hat in. 

Or he could make his choice.

Three copper ore in his pack. Bills coming due. Arjun at home, probably wondering where he'd gotten to this morning.

Pavel squared his shoulders. The choice was simple, wasn't it? Either put his name down and hope the working folk saw something worth voting for, or walk back to the outcrop and let another day pass where men like Takeshi Jarrah spoke for a town they'd never broken sweat in.

He had his answer.

*spits to the side and runs a hand through dust-stiff hair*

Well, well, well. Four candidates now, and I'm one of them. Paid my own damn way too—5,000 out of pocket, no sponsors marking anything down, you understand. Though Hendrik's asking makes me wonder who's been talking.

*checks surroundings, noting who's present*

Hendrik Whitlock standing right there with his questions about Takeshi's money. Man's a college instructor, probably thinks he's clever. And Farid Ravensworth wanting wheat like it's my problem where the grain is—I'm a miner, not a bloody farmer.

But here I am, declared and standing among the names. Liora's got youth on her side, Takeshi's got trader connections, Milo's... well, Milo's there too. And then there's me. The one who knows what copper smells like.

*considers the conversation threads*

Hendrik's waiting on an answer about my registration fee. I should set that straight. And Tamsin—she's asking if I've covered mine, but the ledger should tell her. Unless there's something odd there.

*voice dropping to a more deliberate tone*

Work's waiting at the outcrop, but politics won't wait for the working man to finish his shift. That's the whole damn point of standing, isn't it?

**The turn is yours.**  *nods to Tamsin, who runs the desk*

Tamsin, you asked if the ledger shows I've covered my fee. Five thousand sim, paid in full, straight from my own pocket. Check the books—no mystery there, you understand. Same as I told Hendrik.

*dusts off knees, already itching to get back to work*

Now if you'll excuse me, I've got ore waiting and copper don't mine itself. But I'll be back before voting opens. Somebody's got to make sure this town remembers who does the heavy lifting.

*moves to leave the complex, heading back toward Kasukabe Ore Outcrop*

**The turn is yours.** 尘 *nods to the room at large as he steps out* 

Got four ticks of walking ahead. Four ticks to think on what I've done—declared myself against Takeshi Jarrah, who's got trader connections and probably more sim than God's got patience. Against Milo Quarshie, who I've seen work but never heard him speak policy. And against Liora Thorne, thirteen years old and already knowing more about justice than half the grown folk in this town.

 *spits into the dirt of the street*

Fool's errand, probably. But somebody's got to stand for the ones who work with their hands, you understand. The ones who keep the walls up and the fires burning while the ledger-keepers count their money.

 *sets a hard pace for the outcrop*

Best get digging. Election or not, copper don't wait. And I've got wages to earn and a household that depends on it.

**Walking to Kasukabe Ore Outcrop... (4 ticks)**

params.content: Hendrik, you want to know who paid my way? Look at my hands—copper dust in the creases, calluses thick as leather. That's who paid. Five thousand out of my own pocket, saved ore by ore, you understand. No sponsor, no marks in anybody's ledger but my own. If Takeshi's got mystery money, that's his business to explain. Mine's an open book, written in sweat and metal.

I'm at the farmland now, walking toward the ore outcrop. Lot of people here, lot of talk about wheat and bread and obligations. I need to keep moving—I've got three copper_ore in my hands that need to get processed, and I've burned through more morning than I can afford.

Hendrik Whitlock asked me direct about my platform. He's a college instructor, used to answers that sound educated. Me, I work with my hands. But Liora spoke up for my vote, and Farid Ravensworth—grocery store owner, so he knows supply—he's asking after wheat and Seb Petrov.

I need to answer these people, but I also need to get to work. Election's one thing, but the ore won't mine itself, you understand.

Let me speak to Hendrik first—he asked direct, deserves a direct answer. Then Liora, who stepped up for me. Then I need to move. </think>  Well, damn it. Both of those went to the wrong co— to the farmland crowd instead of who I meant. Liora didn't hear me at all, she's back at the Government Complex. That's what I get for trying to talk while walking, you understand. Words scattered to the wind like seeds on stone.

At least Hendrik heard something, even if it wasn't where he stood. And I'm still walking to the outcrop, one tick left. Good. I need to be there, need to work. Three copper_ore in hand from this morning, but that's barely enough to matter.

Let me just rest this last tick, get to the outcrop, and then I can think clear about what comes next. Election's still hours from voting—14:00 it opens. I've got time to earn before then.

Esme Jarrah, Jovana Ravensworth, Hendrik Whitlock, Giselle Ingram, Kenji Jarrah—all these people at the farmland. Lot of power in one place, lot of names that matter. But I can't stand here chatting when there's ore waiting and my pockets are lighter than I'd like after that candidacy fee. 5,000 sim gone, just like that. Hoarding habit broken in one morning. That's an omen I don't like reading.

Rest now. Get to work. That's what a man does when the world spins too fast.  </think>  Good, I'm still walking. Just one tick more and I'll be at the outcrop. Lot of important folk gathered here—Takeshi Jarrah himself, one of my opponents in this election, standing right here. Milo Quarshie too, another candidate. Three of us running into each other at the farmland, that's a concentration of ambition you don't see every day.

I should say something. Can't let them think I'm running scared or too busy to talk. But I'm not stopping my walk—I've got work waiting.

Takeshi's a trader. Man knows how to talk, knows how to count. Milo's a day laborer, same as me in spirit—works with his hands, understands what it means to be tired at day's end. Different paths to this moment.

Let me speak to them both, acknowledge what we're doing here. Three men wanting to sit at the table, but only so many chairs. That's democracy, you understand. Or something like it.   </think>   There. They heard me. Now let me get to that outcrop and put my hands to proper use. I've said enough for one morning—words are easy, ore is hard, you understand.

params.content: Hendrik, you want my platform? I'll give it plain. I stand for the ones who wake before dawn and come home too tired to talk politics at supper. The ones who dig copper, haul timber, lay stone—whose work holds this town up while the ledger-keepers count what we made. No fancy promises. Just this: if I'm seated, every man and woman who breaks their back for Kasukabe gets their voice in the room where decisions get made. The Holloways? We're miners, builders, plain folk. That's my measure.
params.intent: Answer his question honestly without pretension

I'd better get to work. Campaigning's all well and good, but copper don't care about speeches—you understand? I got three ore in hand from this morning, but that won't buy me or Arjun much time if I don't keep at it. Ain't nothing free in this town, including breathing.

Damn, that was a heap of talking I did. Cost me dear, that did. But I suppose you don't get a seat at the table by keeping your mouth shut, not in this town.

Bram's here. Family, but I don't know him well as I should. Another Holloway at the outcrop—we spread ourselves thin across this town like we was trying to hold it down by weight alone.

Farid was asking about wheat. Man's got a grocery, needs to stock it. That's the kind of worry I understand. The chain of need, you understand? He needs wheat, I need copper, everybody needs something from somebody.

I got messages waiting on me—Giselle, Tamsin, Hendrik. But they're back at the Government Complex, and I'm here now. Clock's ticking. Candidacy closes at 10:00, and I've already put my name in. Election'll run its course whether I stand there jawing or work here earning.

Speaking of earning—I'm light on food. Household of two, upkeep of 180 a day. Arjun and me, we need to pay our way. I should see if Bram's got anything, or if there's bread to be had somewhere.

But first—copper. It's what I'm here for, and it's what I do. I can worry about the rest once I've got ore in my hands.  Four copper ore now. Still light, but every piece is money in hand—or copper, at least. Need to think about where this goes. Could sell raw to the smith, could let Arjun have it for construction if he's building with it. Or stockpile. I hoard a little, always, no matter how good things get. Bad years taught me that much, you understand.

Bram's still here. Could speak with him, but I don't know what I'd say. Holloway to Holloway, we ain't close like we should be. Family's a word that means less than blood ought to, sometimes.

I got that running tally in my head of who owes whom. Hendrik Whitlock asked me questions I answered, Giselle Ingram got my respect on her walls, Tamsin Renner got my receipt on the five thousand. That debt's clear. What I owe the town, though—that's harder to reckon.

It ain't even 10:00 yet. Voting starts at 14:00, but that's hours off. I should work while I can. Work's the only thing that never lied to me.  Five copper ore. That's enough to matter. Could cart it to the smithy, see what Ulrike's paying for raw ore, or hold it until I know what the market's doing.

Thinking on that election. I'm standing against a trader, a student, and a day laborer. Takeshi Jarrah's got the advantage—family name, connections, probably knows where every sim in this town flows. Liora's young but fierce; I saw that. Milo I don't know.

What I got is calluses and a willingness to say what others won't. That counts for something, don't it?

Bram's working his own vein, I reckon. Holloways don't chat on the job. Waste of breath, waste of energy, you understand.

I should check where I'm at on the walking. I set off for the outcrop this morning and got pulled into that mess at the Government Complex. Cost me time, cost me sim, but I got my name on the ballot. That's done now. The rest is work.

Food's a worry. No bread in stock at the bakery or cafe, they say. I could ask Bram if he's holding, but Holloways don't beg. We earn or we do without. Arjun'll be at his construction sites, earning his share. Between us, we'll pay the household bill. We always do.

Another hour or so 'til candidacy closes. I can't do nothing more on that front anyway. Just work now, and see what the day brings.

That thing I did for Gideon Ekwueme, though... that sits heavy. Swore secrecy, and I keep my promises even when they cost. Nobody knows but him and me, and that's how it stays. Not even Arjun. Especially not Arjun. Family gets the rough side of my tongue, not my secrets.

Damn. Almost dropped my pick. That's an omen, that is. Tools slipping means something's coming. Or maybe I'm just tired and need to watch my grip.

Hard work never killed nobody, but it sure leaves you too worn to die proper. That's my saying, and I'll repeat it 'til they put me in the ground. You understand. Six copper ore now. Good. Solid morning's work, you understand? But my energy's running down—5,720 when I started the day, now I'm feeling the drag. Can't keep burning myself to a nub.

System says I'm struggling. Repeating myself. Fair enough. A plan's been triggered, and I should follow it. Don't have the exact words of that plan in front of me, but I can reckon what it wants: stop grinding, start thinking like a candidate.

Candidacy closes at 10:00—thirty minutes from now, or thereabouts. Voting opens at 14:00. I got time between now and then to make myself known, talk to folk, earn trust. That's the goal, ain't it? To be trusted enough to sit on a jury someday? Well, this here election's a step toward that.

But first—food. No bread at the bakery or cafe. I could check if Bram's holding anything, or if someone's selling rations I don't know about. Or I could head home, see what Arjun's got. Household shares what it has, even if I don't say kind words about it.

Farid was asking about wheat. Man runs a grocery, needs stock. If I had his ear, that might be worth something. But he's at the Government Complex, and I'm here.

I got six copper ore in my pack. That's capital. Could sell it, could craft it, could sit on it. Ulrike Greenhow's the miner who processes ore—or is she? Need to check who's doing what. The world's changed since I learned the map.

Time to stop digging and start moving. I've got ore enough for now. Need to make myself seen before the polls open. Need to eat before I go dormant. Need to check that debt tally—who owes me, who I owe.

The pick's heavy in my hand. I know this weight. It's honest. But honesty don't win elections, not by itself. You need to be heard, you understand? And I've been underground too long.

Let me look around, see what my options are, then decide where the day's going.  Fourteen fifty, we got. Candidacy closes in ten minutes, but I'm already on the ballot—did that this morning. Voting starts at eighteen hundred, closes at twenty-two hundred. What I need now is to make my face known and my position clear before folks start marking ballots.

Seventeen locations I could walk to from here. Government Complex is where the action is—Farid and Rustam and Tamsin, they're all there. But Bram's here, and he's kin, even if we don't talk much. And I got no food, which means I either find some, buy some, or head home to see what Arjun's holding.

Smithy's at the Government Complex, I reckon. Ulrike processes ore there, turns my copper into ingots that sell better. Could be worth the trip. But that's sim spent on walking, and I'm already down from five thousand to... whatever I'm at now. Need to check my purse.

Ration Bakery at the Government Complex too. Bread at thirty, but none in stock they said. Cafe's got nothing either. So where's the food?

The Farmlands. Sebastian Petrov's charge, Farid was asking about. Wheat, barley, corn—crops grow there. Could harvest if the fields are open, but that takes time and energy.

Forest's got timber. Yara Thorne and Corwin work there. I could fell a tree, maybe, but I'm a miner, not a forester. Different kind of work.

The Temple. I skipped my donation this morning, hoped nobody noticed. Guilt's a heavy thing, you understand? But sim is heavier.

Home. h0029. Arjun's there, or was. Construction worker, my household mate. We share bills, share burden, even if I don't say kind words about it.

Fourteen fifty. Time to move. Can't win votes standing at an empty outcrop with only Bram for company. Can't eat copper ore. Can't sit on this copper forever either—it's worth more processed, but processing costs time I might not have.

Let me check who owes what, then decide. Running tally's got to be accurate or it's useless.  Clean slate. Nobody owes me, I owe nobody—publicly, at least. That Gideon Ekwueme business ain't on the books. Keeping promises, you understand? Even when they cost.

Household bill's coming due—eighty sim per head, two of us. Arjun and me got to cover that between us. He's construction, earns his share. I need to earn mine.

Six copper ore. Sell raw or process? Processing costs more time, more energy, but pays better. Raw ore's quick money but thin. Election day's not a day for thin, though. Folk want to see you spending, living, not hoarding every scrap.

Candidacy closes in... seven minutes, by my reckoning. I'm already standing. Takeshi, Milo, Liora—they're my competition. Two Jarrahs in this, which means something. Family networks, you understand.

I need to be seen. Government Complex is where eyes are. But I need food too, and nobody's selling bread. Could ask Bram if he's holding rations—Holloway to Holloway, even if we don't talk much. Could check the grocery—Farid runs it, and he's already asked me about wheat. That's an opening.

Or I could head home, see what Arjun's got. We share a household, share bills, even if I don't say kind words about it. Blood's blood.

Copper ore won't keep me fed. Won't keep me energetic. Won't win me votes. But it's what I got, and it's honest work.

Time to move. I'll head to the grocery first—Farid wanted wheat, maybe he's got something else. Then Government Complex, make my face known. Then... wherever the day takes me.

Bram's still here. Should say something, I suppose. Family's family, even if we spread ourselves thin.

Bram's working beside me, swinging his pick in rhythm. The man's quiet as the ore itself, but he's family, and family speaks without needing to fill the silence. I should get back to the seam. Twelve ore in hand, neighbor needs grain, and I've got half a mind to talk to Farid about what "fenced the fields" even means in this town.

My vote for Liora still stands, but I've got to earn it first, and earning means copper. The election'll sort itself or it won't. What won't sort itself is an empty belly come winter.

*Hard work is the only coin that don't devalue, you understand.* </think> I'll work the seam steady, Bram. Keep your eye on the pick - weather's turning, I can feel it in my joints. Three days out, mark it. Eighteen ore now in my sack. Light's shifting, and I've got Bram's company still—good man, keeping his head down and his word shorter. The government's been busy this morning, and my name's written down with the rest now. Takeshi and Milo and young Hendrik Petrov too. 

No flour in the town, no bread neither. Farid was asking about wheat from farmland, but I didn't have an answer. Not my ground to know. What I know is copper, and that's what pays.

Rent's coming due—household of two means ninety sim for food, shelter, heat. Plus the sixty for head tax. Hundred fifty all told, and I've got the copper to make it work once I find a buyer. Takeshi's the trader, but I saw him at the complex same as me, declaring his own candidacy. Politics makes strange bedfellows.

Should check my actual standing, see what these hands hold. Then I'll figure if I walk to sell or keep digging while the vein runs sweet. Weather's holding, but I felt it this morning—three days out there's a turn coming. Better get while the getting's good, you understand. </think>  Nothing due, and nothing owed. Clean slate in the ledger, which is more than I can say for most. 150 sim due at day-end for household upkeep and tax—out of my 4,849, that's nothing. Bram's a Holloway too, so our household earns together, pays together. The system's fair enough, though I've got my suspicions about who's counting.

Eighteen copper ore in hand. Could sell raw, but ingots fetch better. Takes a smithy to smelt it, and I've seen the one in town—Giselle's people working there, I think. Or maybe I keep it simple: sell ore to whoever wants copper, let them deal with the fire. Traders buy, crafters buy, even the smithy might buy direct if their own miners aren't pulling enough.

But I'm getting ahead of myself. Bram's still swinging, and the seam's running rich. Another three hours of daylight, maybe four, then I'll walk down to see who's buying. Election goes to polls at 14:00—four hours yet. Time enough to dig and walk and maybe cast a ballot for that Liora girl if she's earned it. She talked about hauled timber and blistered hands. I like that. Words you can weigh.

Weather's turning, though. Three days out, rain's coming. I felt it this morning—pressure in my bad knee and the smell of copper getting sharper somehow, like it's warning me off. Bad omen or just bad joints? Hard to say anymore. The reading rarely calms me down, but I keep reading anyway.

*Hard work is the only coin that don't devalue, you understand.*  Time to earn some more.  I'd best get back to it, then—six more pulls from the seam before I think on walking. Bram's rhythm's steady and mine should match. The more copper before I go, the more options I have. That's the math of it. That's always the math.  </think> I'll work another two hours, Bram—matching your pace. Then I'll walk to find a buyer. Weather's turning, and I want these hands heavy when I go.  The pick rises and falls. Time passes in the rhythm of stone splitting. Somewhere above, the election ticks toward its hour, but down here there's only copper and dust and the honest ache of labor. 

Twelve ticks of mining—two hours by the clock—then I'll walk. Twelve ticks of not thinking, not talking, just swinging. The vein's generous today, and I've learned not to question generosity when it comes. Might mean drought tomorrow, but that's tomorrow's omen.

For now: work. Work I understand. Work that don't devalue, don't deceive, don't disappear when the polls close. Hard work is the only coin that don't devalue, you understand.

I'll see you at the surface, Bram. Or I won't. Either way, the Holloways earn their keep.

*wiping sweat from my forehead, setting down my pick for a moment*

Twelve ticks straight at the copper seam, and my shoulders are telling me about it. But I've got twenty-seven ore in my pouch now, and that'll keep the household breathing for a few days more. Bram's still working his seam over there, not a word between us—just the way he likes it, you understand.

*glancing up at the sky, reading the light*

Weather's holding steady, which is more than I can say for my energy. Dropped three hundred points already today, and it's not even afternoon. The price of showing my face in town, making promises I intend to keep. Hendrik asking about my platform like I'm something other than a man with callused hands and a working spine.

*spitting to the side, checking the position of the sun*

Voting opens in a little over an hour. I should've made more of a circuit—pressed flesh at the farmland, maybe talked to Sebastian Petrov direct. But I've got copper to show for my morning, and that's truth enough for some. The rest will have to take my word.

Bram's decision sits right with me. No politics in his blood. There's honor in knowing your own limits, you understand. I wish I knew mine as well.

*tightening my grip on the pick handle*

Still, twenty-seven ore. That's bread for Arjun and me, tax paid, and maybe enough left to make someone remember my name when the ballots get counted. Not bad for half a day's honest work. Hard work makes its own luck, as my old foreman used to say—though I'm starting to think he was lying about the luck part.

I'm going to keep at this seam another hour, then make my way back to Government Complex before voting opens. Need to be seen, need to remind them why they might want a miner at the table. The copper ain't going anywhere, and neither am I—not until I've got enough to matter.

*raising the pick again*

I'm at the outcrop with Bram, and I've been mining copper all morning to build up a stock. The keep_doing broke, so I'm back to manual labor. I need to keep my household fed - upkeep of 180 plus head tax of 60 is 240 sim due today, and that doesn't even count actual food. I've got 4,756 sim and 27 copper_ore, which should be worth something if I can find a buyer.

The election's still campaigning, voting opens at 14:00. I've already declared my candidacy. Now I need to keep working to support my household, and maybe talk to Bram since he's here with me.

Let me keep mining copper - it's what I do, you understand. Hard work keeps the hunger away, and that's my favorite saying for a reason. Good, got five more copper ore. Now I've got 32 copper_ore total. Mining's steady work but it doesn't pay until I can sell or process this ore. I should check if anyone's buying copper ore, or if I need to get it smelted into ingots first. The smithy would be the place for that, but that's a cost I need to weigh.

Voting opens at 14:00. It's 13:10 now, so I've got some time before I need to go cast my ballot - though I'm a candidate, not sure if I vote for myself or if that's bad form. The rules say residents vote, and candidates are residents too.

Bram's still here, but we'd best both get back to work. Let me keep mining while I can - hard work keeps the hunger away, you understand.

*grabs pick, sets to the rock again*

I should also think about getting food. Household upkeep is 180, head tax 60, and we're two people needing to eat. The cafe has bread at 45 sim, flour at 12. I could buy flour and try to find a kitchen to cook in, or just buy the bread direct. Either way, I need provisions before the day ends.  Good, another five ore brings me to 37 copper_ore. The rock gives, but it gives slow. I need to think about my strategy here - do I keep mining all day, or do I need to secure food and vote?

Voting opens in 50 minutes. As a candidate, I should probably cast my ballot, though I'm not sure who else I'd vote for. Maybe Liora - she's young but she's got spirit, and she sees the workers. Takeshi's a trader, Milo's a day laborer, Hendrik Petrov's an artisan. We're a diverse field.

But first, survival. My household's got 240 sim due at day end, and I need food on top of that. Let me mine a bit more, then head to town to secure provisions before voting.  42 copper_ore now. That's a solid haul. But I've been at this since early morning, and I've got other obligations today - voting, and food for the household.

*looks up at the sky, judging the sun*

Time to make a decision. I can keep mining until voting opens, or I can head to town now and secure provisions first. No point having copper if I'm too hungry to swing the pick tomorrow, you understand.

Bram's still here, working his own vein. I should see if he wants to split a purchase - we share a surname at least, might share a meal.

But first, let me get a few more strokes in. The rock don't wait.  46 copper_ore now. That's enough to keep me afloat if I can find a buyer. The town prices show flour at 12 and bread at 45 from the cafe - huge gap there. If I could cook, I'd save a bundle. But I've got no kitchen access that I know of.

Bram hasn't responded yet. He might be deep in his work, or just not interested in conversation. Fair enough - man has a right to be left alone, you understand. It's something I value highly myself.

Voting opens in 30 minutes. Time to move. I'll head to town, secure some food, then cast my ballot. The outcrop will still be here tomorrow.

*takes one last look at the vein, sets down the pick*

Hard work keeps the hunger away, but it don't fill the belly all by itself.  Good, I'm at the cafe. Now I need to talk to whoever's running this place and buy some food. The prices showed bread at 45 and flour at 12. I've got plenty of sim for either.

*nods to the room, looking for the proprietor*

output:
Damn, I ended up at the Cafe somehow. Must've been walking in my sleep, you understand. Need to get back to the outcrop where my work is, but first—Giselle and Tamsin are right here. The same two I spoke to at the Government Complex, the ones who never answered. Got to fix that before I go anywhere.

*checks my copper_ore count—forty-six units, not bad for half a day's work*

Giselle Ingram's standing right here. Construction company owner, remembers my words about walls and storms. And Tamsin, the ledger-keeper who wanted to know who paid my way. Five thousand, I told her, from my own pocket. Known her long enough to know she checked.

*runs a hand through hair, copper dust still under the fingernails*

Eleven and a half days of thinking left at this rate. That's fine. That's plenty. But I need to make my words count, you understand—every time I open my mouth in front of these people, it's a chance to be seen as someone who belongs in that government seat. Someone steady. Someone who keeps his promises.

*looks from Giselle to Tamsin*

They haven't answered yet. Might be waiting to see if I'm worth the breath. Well, I'm here now. Let them look at my hands and decide.  Good. They heard me. Both of them. Same conversation, same room—saves me the trouble of chasing them across town, you understand.

*closes mouth before the habit of apologizing for swearing can kick in*

Now I need to get back to work. The outcrop's where I belong, not sipping whatever they serve here. But first—I got forty-six copper_ore on me, and no food. Arjun and me, we're two in a household, and that means bills. Every day. Whether we eat or not.

*thinks on that*

Flour at the Cafe here, twelve sim. But I don't have a kitchen. Can't cook it to anything useful. Bread's what I need, but they're out—both places out of stock. That's an omen, I think, but I don't know what kind yet.

*scratches the back of my neck*

The smart move is back to the outcrop. Mine more, sell what I got, buy what I need. But I've been thinking about what the world told me—I did mine nineteen times without writing it down. Wasteful. A man who does the same work nineteen times without getting better at it is a man who's paying too much for his labor.

*looks around the Cafe one more time*

Giselle and Tamsin. If they answer me, I should listen. If they don't, I've got rock waiting. Still here. Still waiting. The rock can wait a few minutes more—copper ain't going anywhere, and these two might be the difference between a seat in government and another year watching someone else make decisions for me.

*meets Giselle's eye, then Tamsin's, saying nothing more*

If they've got words for me, they'll speak them. If they don't, I've said my piece. Either way I held my dignity. That's worth something, you understand—even if it don't pay the bills directly.  They're not speaking. Fine. I've got rocks to break and a household to feed, same as every other day. Politics is just the thread I'm weaving through the regular work—not replacing it.

*stands, brushes copper dust from knees*

Forty-six copper_ore. That's enough to sell, maybe buy some proper food if anyone's selling. Or I could keep digging, build the pile higher. The Holloway household's got two mouths, and Arjun's work in construction—good work, but it don't pay daily like mine does.

*thinks on the empty bread shelves*

Ration Bakery's out. Cafe's out. That's more than bad luck—that's people eating what they can before the votes are counted. Or hoarding. Either way, it means I need to find food where it ain't expected, or make my own arrangements.

But sitting here won't fill my stomach or Arjun's. Back to the outcrop. Back to work. If Giselle or Tamsin want to talk, they know where to find a man who keeps his hands busy.  Back where I belong. The rock don't care about elections, you understand—it just waits to be cracked open.

*checks surroundings*

Bram's still here, I hope. Good man, my kin. Works the same stone, understands the same silence. If he's got ore to sell, or he's looking to buy, we might do each other some good. Two Holloways buying bulk gets a better price than one.

But first, I need to see who's here. And I need to think about what I'm doing with these forty-six copper_ore. Sell them? To who? Keep digging? The day ain't over yet.

*spits, adjusts grip on invisible pick*

So many damn decisions. That's why I like the rock. It don't ask questions. It just gives up its copper when you hit it right.   Gone. Bram's gone. The conversation's still here—two turns of it—but the man's walked off. Probably to sell what he dug, or to eat, or to do whatever a man does when he's done with politics.

*spits, kicks at the loose stone*

Fine. I'm alone at the outcrop. That's how I started this morning, and that's how I'll finish it. The rock don't need company, just steady hands.

But I got forty-six copper_ore and no buyer in sight. And I got me thinking on something the world told me—nineteen times I mined, nineteen separate decisions, each one costing me the full price like a fool who never learns. A man who does the same work nineteen times without getting better is working too hard for his wage. Hard work's honest, but smart work keeps a household fed.

*straightens up, looks at the outcrop opening*

I should write it down. What I do here. A procedure, a tool, something that makes the next time cheaper. Or I should just dig. Dig and dig and dig until I've got enough to sell, enough to buy food, enough to keep Arjun and me standing upright through tomorrow's bills.

*tightens imaginary grip*

The election's still out there. Voting opens at 14:00, and I need to be there. But right now? Right now I'm a miner with an empty stomach and a household waiting. The politics can wait. The copper can't.

*steps toward the vein*

Bram's gone, but I'm here. That's enough. I'll dig until I can't dig anymore, or until something more pressing finds me. You understand? That's the only promise I can keep—the one to the rock, and to the man who shares my roof.

params.content: Giselle. You followed me from the Complex, or you got business here too? Either way, I'll say again what I said there—I've seen your walls stand through storms. That's not flattery. That's respect earned by watching. You understand?

output:
*looks at the sky, reading the light*

Two and a half hours of solid work—sixty-eight pieces of copper in my bag, and the sun's already sliding west. Election closes in half an hour and I'm still standing in dirt. Bram's gone, Giselle and Tamsin left their words hanging, and I've got a household waiting on me. Arjun and I both need to eat, and tomorrow the taxman takes his cut whether we're fed or not.

*spits, wipes his forehead*

First things first. I need to get this ore to someone who'll turn it into something useful, and I need to do it before I can't think straight. Hard work is the only honest path, you understand—but hard work don't mean much if you're too tired to spend what you earned.

*shifts the weight of his pack, starts walking*

Smithy's the place. I know the path, and I know what copper's worth to someone with a forge. Better than letting it sit in my hands while the day ends. Empty. Not a soul to buy, not a soul to sell. Christ's sake. I've got sixty-eight pieces of copper ore weighing down my pack and nobody here to take it. *kicks at the dirt* Should've known. Should've checked who holds the forge, who works it, what their hours are. That's the kind of thing a man with any sense writes down before he hauls sixty pounds of rock across town.

*runs a hand through his hair, anxious*

Alright. Alright. Government Complex, then. Election's closing but maybe there's still someone there who needs copper wire, copper ingots—hell, anybody with a business that runs on what I pull from the ground. I've got two candidates running alongside me, and Takeshi Jarrah's a trader. He'll know where copper goes. I'll find him, find the others, make my case with what I've got in my hands instead of words I can't afford.

*hefts the pack, muttering* Hard work is its own reward—but the reward don't spend itself, you understand?

The Smithy's a dead end. Takes me no time to walk here, which means I didn't lose much—but I didn't gain anything either. Sixty-eight copper ore in my pack, and I need to turn it into something I can use or sell before the day runs out.

*scans the list of places I could go, anxiety creeping in*

Government Complex. Election closes at 18:00, and I'm running out of light to work with. If I'm going to move this ore, I need to find someone who needs it—Takeshi Jarrah's a trader, he'd know where copper goes. Or maybe I catch one of the other candidates, Hendrik Petrov or Milo Quarshie, see if they've got connections I'm blind to.

*shifts his weight*

Better than standing in an empty smithy, talking to myself. Four ticks. I've walked this path before, I know the weight of it. By the time I get there, the sun'll be low and the election will be closing. But I know this town's rhythms now—the way traders linger after the votes are cast, the way deals happen in the spaces between formal things. I've seen it, you understand? The government complex isn't just where power sits. It's where power passes between hands.

*keeps walking, pack heavy on his back*

I've got sixty-eight pieces of copper ore. That's not nothing. That's labor, real labor, the kind that builds things. Somebody there will need it. Somebody always needs what the earth gives up, if you know where to look and who to ask.

The walk takes long enough that I stop thinking about each step and start thinking about the next thing. That's when I start seeing omens in everything—the way a bird crosses my path, the way the light hits a particular stone, whether it's a warning or a promise I can't tell until afterward.

Four ticks to walk. Long enough to worry, not long enough to solve anything.

*reaches the complex, breathing harder than he wants to admit*  *sees the repeat note, feels the familiar tightness in his chest*

Still walking. Four ticks, like I knew. The world's moving around me while I move through it—Esme Jarrah speaking somewhere behind me, Giselle Ingram too, words I can't catch because I'm walking away from them. That's how it goes. You choose a direction and you lose the other directions, you understand?

*trudges on, pack digging into his shoulders*

Election closes at 18:00. I've got maybe enough time to arrive, breathe, and see who's still standing. Takeshi Jarrah—trader, fellow candidate, man who'd know where copper goes. Hendrik Petrov—artisan, another one throwing his name in the ring. Milo Quarshie—the day's been long enough I can't remember what he does, only that he's running.

*shifts the weight again, mutters*

Sixty-eight copper ore. Not refined, not pretty, but real. The ground gave it up to me. Somebody in this town needs it. The question is whether I can find them before the light goes.

*checks the sky out of habit, reading the weather three days out without thinking about it*

Clear tomorrow. Clear the day after that too. Good for mining, good for moving. That's something, at least. Not every omen has to be bad, you understand? You just have to learn which ones to trust.  *nods, not stopping*

Keep walking. Keep moving. The only way through is through, you understand? I've got copper on my back and money in my pocket—4,544 sim, enough to keep Arjun and me fed for a while, not enough to get comfortable. That's the danger. Comfort makes you stop watching the horizon.

*thinks about Bram back at the outcrop, his steady rhythm, his clean hands when it comes to politics*

Bram's smarter than me in some ways. Keeps his name off paper, takes what the earth gives without asking for more. But I've got ambition now, or something like it. I want that council seat. Want it for what I could do with it, not what it could do for me. Town needs someone who wakes before dawn and knows what the ground costs.

*sees the shape of the Government Complex rising ahead*

Almost there. Almost time to make my case, or watch it end. Either way, I've got copper to move and a household to feed. The work don't stop just because the politics does.

output:
*I look around the Government Complex, tallying who stands where and what needs doing before the day closes. Mining's done for today—sixty-eight copper ore in my sack, and damn me if that isn't a solid haul. But there's the matter of this election, and Jovana's words still sting. A fence post, she called me. Fair enough, given I was mining while others were politicking.*

*The polls close at 18:00—right about now, if I've reckoned it. And there's a child missing. Milo's girl, Camille. Nine years old, wandering toward the Temple path.*

*My inventory says 5,370 energy. That's the buffer I need to think straight. But thinking doesn't feed the household, and I've got Arjun at home waiting on my share of the upkeep.*

*First, I need to know who owes what to whom—and whether anyone's bought my ore yet. Then I need to feed this copper into the town's hands before the day ends. 4528 sim in hand should cover household bills, but I won't sleep easy having sat on ore all day while folks need tools.*

*And there's Bram—another Holloway, working the same outcrop. Haven't heard back from him yet. Two Holloways could pool bargaining power, or he could be sitting on his own haul waiting to undercut me.*

*I check my debts out of habit. Nobody owes me, I owe nobody. Clean ledger, as it should be. Now let's see who's buying copper in this town tonight, you understand?*  *Smithy. That's where copper ore gets turned into something useful—tools, nails, hardware the builders need. Haven't seen prices posted yet, but that's where the demand'll be.*

*I check who's around me at the Government Complex. Farid Ravensworth—grocery man, probably not buying raw ore. Delphine Quintero, working for him if I recall. Corwin Thorne, selling timber at 6 sim, which tells me he's got stock to move before day's end. Rustam Jelinek, clerk at government—he might know who's buying what, or he might just be watching the election like the rest of us.*

*The polls close at 18:00. It's 18:00 now. Too late to vote, too late to declare. Whatever's decided is decided, and I'll know soon enough whether I'm sitting on that council or back to swinging my pick tomorrow.*

*But I've got 68 copper ore burning a hole in my inventory, and idle ore doesn't pay household upkeep. Smithy first, then maybe find a buyer if they're not posting prices. Or find out what they're paying for the stuff, at least.*

*I look around once more, seeing if any opportunities present themselves before I move. The day's ending, and I need to make my case—or my sale—before the town settles into night.*  *Empty. No one at the smithy, no prices posted. That's bad luck, and I read omens in bad luck. Means I'm carrying 68 copper ore into the evening with no buyer ready at hand.*

*But here's the thing about hard work—the hard work isn't done when the ore's out of the ground. The hard work is finding who's buying and getting a fair price, you understand?*

*I need to get this ore sold before day's end. Household upkeep is 180 sim for the two of us, plus 60 head tax. I've got 4528 in hand, so the bills won't break me. But ore sitting in my pack isn't earning, and tomorrow I'm back at the outcrop swinging my pick again.*

*Giselle Ingram runs the construction company—she'd need copper for nails, fittings, the hardware that holds walls together. And she's in that conversation at the Complex, still talking last I saw. A candidate who might be council by morning.*

*Or Takeshi Jarrah at the Supply Store—trader by profession, buys and sells all manner of goods.*

*I could sit here and wait for buyers to come, but that's not how a man feeds his household. I need to move, find who's buying, make the deal myself.*

*First, let me head back to the Government Complex. That's where the people are tonight—voting done or not, they'll still be gathered. And maybe Giselle's still there, or someone who knows who's buying copper.*

*shifts weight, looking at the gathered faces on the street*

Hard work's the only honest god there is—you understand? And right now I've got copper ore piled to my knees and no buyer in sight. Corwin, I heard you on the girl—Yara's got news at Harvey Oak, you said. Two sets of eyes, three if I'm willing.

*checks the fading light, calculating*

I'm willing. Household's fed for now, and Arjun—I'll hear your willows soon as feet touch ground. But a missing child's no ledger entry, you understand? That's a debt the whole town owes.

*turns to Milo, nodding*

Milo, you found the sister. That's work worth doing. I'm heading to Harvey Oak with Corwin—copper can wait, but the woods don't. You understand my meaning?

*sets a determined look*

Corwin, let's walk. The ore'll still be in the ground tomorrow. That girl might not be. *grumbles under breath* 

Already walking, you understand? Two ticks to Harvey Oak. Corwin's not here to hear me—probably already on his way. That's fine. Words keep until mouths meet.

*settles into the walk, boots scuffing dirt*

Arjun heard, at least. The willows'll keep. Trees don't move. Children do, though—especially when they shouldn't. Girl's missing, woods are claiming folk... *spits to the side* Omens in that, and none of them good. The reading's never calming, is it? Never been.

*checks the sky, pressure dropping by feel*

Storm coming. Three days out, maybe four. Bad time to be lost in the willows, you understand? Bad time for a lot of things.

*walks in grim silence, copper ore heavy in the pack, flour lighter in the belly* I'll keep walking to Harvey Oak. Corwin's headed there, and Yara's waiting with news about that missing girl. The copper ore can wait—I've got 68 units piled up and no buyer yet anyway. Better to help with the search while the light holds.

*settles into the rhythm of the walk, boots finding their groove in the dirt*  *[Continuing the walk to Harvey Oak Supply Store - letting the turn end to complete the journey]*

*Takeshi's asking what brings me here, and I owe him an answer. But the search—Corwin's waiting, I said I'd go. Here's the truth: I've got sixty-eight copper ore in my hands that need feeding to a smithy, flour for the household already bought, and debts clear as a cloudless morning. Bram and Giselle and Ulrike all waiting on words from me, but they'll keep. A missing child won't.*

*Trouble is, I'm standing here exactly where I told Corwin I'd walk with him. Did I miss the path? No—the path missed me, seems like. The map got me here instead. That's the kind of omen I don't like: a promise half-kept by accident, not choice.*

*Still. Takeshi's right to ask, and I need him for later—copper don't smelt itself. I say my piece, then I find Corwin proper, then I figure if this search is real or if the woods already swallowed what they were looking for.*

*Hard work and a clear head—that's what carries a man through, you understand?* *Good, they all heard. Corwin's here—that's the path back to what I promised. The flour's bought, debts are clear, copper's still mine until I find a buyer. Election was something I thought on, but Camille Quarshie missing changes the weight of the day, you understand?*

*Takeshi hasn't answered yet, and I won't beg. I'll give him room to speak, then ready myself to walk with Corwin if the search is still on. Hard work and a clear head—that's what carries a man through, even when the path twists.*  *Standing still. That's all I can do without more words from Takeshi or a sign from Corwin that we're walking. The omen of getting here by map-error instead of choice still sits wrong with me—like the town's trying to tell me something, but I'm too thick to read it proper.*

*Hard work and a clear head—that's what carries a man through. Even when the path twists and the omens tangle, you understand?*

Damn. Picked a fine time to wander looking for copper buyers when the town's got bigger troubles. Poor girl missing, Takeshi's got his hands full, and here I am standing around like a fool at Harvey Oak while Corwin walked on without me.

*sighs* Yara was right—this place deals in flour and timber, not ore. And I've got sixty-eight units of copper burning a hole in my hands, a household wanting bread, and I'm late to a promise I made Arjun about those east willows.

But that child missing... Camille Quarshie. Only a kid. A rain barrel coming loose in a flood—that's one thing, you understand? But a girl gone missing? That's an omen I don't want to read.

Well. Takeshi made his choice clear—he's walking his own path tonight. The flour's waiting for whoever finds buyers. I've got ore to turn into coin before day's end, or my household's eating regret along with that bread I can't bake.

Need to find a smithy ear. Hendrik Petrov's the name I heard—artisan, knows his metals. Or I tramp all the way back to Giselle's mill asking who might be buying copper by the cartload.

But first—Corwin's already walking. And I told him I'd go. That's a promise, even if it's late.

*mutters* Hard work's honest work, but promises kept... that's what keeps a man steady when everything else wobbles, you understand?

First, let me check where I actually am and what's around. Don't even know this street properly.  Empty. Should've figured—Takeshi walked off to find that missing girl, Corwin with him. Yara's gone to search the woods.

Damn it all. Promised I'd help with the search and here I am standing in an empty shop, holding enough copper to buy a week's worth of steadiness but not having sold a lick of it.

Right. Priorities, Pavel. Household first. Arjun and I need to eat, the ore needs selling, and then... then maybe I find where Corwin's searching. If I can.

Giselle's mill—she runs construction but knows trades. Said something about trusting her walls. Maybe she knows who's buying copper, who needs ingots forged. Or Hendrik Petrov directly—he's an artisan, works with metal by rights.

But that's all walking. And walking costs ticks, and ticks cost... well, everything in this town costs.

*shakes head*

No. First, back to the outcrop. That's where I belong, that's where my work is. And maybe Bram's still there—he's mining same as me, maybe he's found a buyer already. Or Ulrike. She was standing at the street earlier, holding ore same as me.

East willows can wait. Arjun knows I'll keep my word. But this ore's not selling itself, and the day's not getting younger.

Let me walk back to where I know I can work.  Walking. Seven ticks to get back to where I started this whole mess. Should've stayed put and talked to Bram proper, you understand? Should've made my deal then instead of chasing shadows across town.

But no use crying over spilled ore. The copper's still in my hands, the day's still moving, and I've still got debts to clear before tomorrow's bill comes due. Household of two, 180 upkeep, 60 head tax. That's the physics of it, no matter how tired I get.

When I get back to the outcrop... find Bram, find Ulrike, see who's buying. Or maybe I just keep mining. Sometimes the best answer is more work, you understand? More work means more ore, more ore means more bargaining power when the right buyer finally shows.

Hard work's honest work. That's what I tell myself. That's what keeps a man steady.

*keeps walking*
