output:
Pavel feels the familiar itch between his shoulder blades—too many people, too much talking, and not a single copper ore sold yet. Sixty-eight units sitting heavy in his hands, and every path to profit seems to fork the wrong way.

He fidgets with his pocket, where he keeps the running tally. Debts owed, debts held. The numbers ground him. But what unsettles him now isn't the copper—it's the feeling that something's off about this whole day. The missing girl, the election circus, the way everyone suddenly wants something from him. An omen? No. Just bad luck stacking up like unpaid bills.

Jovana's still waiting on him. Fourteen ticks ago she spoke, and he's let her hang like a fool. But she mentioned wheat and flour both, and he's holding neither. The election's tomorrow, polls open at 14:00, and he's been running his mouth more than his pickaxe.

"Takeshi," he mutters to himself, not that anyone asked. "Sixty-eight copper, and he talks about flour and timber like they're the same damn thing."

He needs to sell this ore before the day's out. The smithy at the outcrop—that's where the fire is. But he'd promised Corwin help with the search, and now he's standing here while the sun sinks, talking to traders instead of walking with foresters. His word, given. His word, slipping.

The right thing and the smart thing, pulling different directions. Story of his life, you understand. The copper sits in his hands—sixty-eight units, each one dug with sweat and the knowledge that the blight might come again, might take this too. Takeshi will answer or he won't. But Pavel's not standing here past dark like a post begging for conversation.

He pictures Arjun at home, probably already wondering where the flour is, where the ore money is, why his brother's word stretches thinner every election season. The east willows wait. Promises stack up like ore unsold, and each one pulls him a different direction.

The right to be left alone. He holds to that. But tonight, holding it means moving—selling, earning, keeping the household bill paid. Not standing in a crowd hoping someone needs what he's got.

Jovana's mark is still open. Bram's here—maybe Bram's the buyer. But Bram's family, and family business gets complicated. Better a stranger's hand with clean reckonings.

He tightens his grip on the copper and waits one breath. Takeshi speaks or he walks. No more chasing conversations like a dog after scraps. The work is at the outcrop. The money is wherever someone will pay. The missing girl is Corwin's burden now—Pavel's word bent, but not yet broken.

Hard work is its own reward, he tells himself, the old saying scraping his throat. But hard work without pay is just sweating for free, you understand? And he didn't come to Kasukabe to sweat for free.

One tick. Two. The evening stretches. Either answer now, or he moves.  Pavel grinds his teeth—a habit he learned early and never unlearned. Already walking, yes, but four ticks still to go, and every tick a man could be buying, could be selling, could be earning. Instead he's in motion without arriving, the worst kind of state.

The street is thick with people whose names he mostly knows and whose business he mostly doesn't trust. Jovana still waiting on him, fourteen ticks and counting. Ulrike with her own copper, maybe looking to sell, maybe looking to undercut. Bram, blood but not always ally.

He could stop walking. Rest here, work the crowd, find his buyer before the sun settles completely. The outcrop will wait. The outcrop always waits—it's been waiting ten years since his blistered hands first gripped a pickaxe there.

But standing means talking, and talking means spending sim he hasn't earned yet on words that haven't produced a sale. The old anxiety hums in his chest: what if they don't need miners next season? What if the ore runs thin, what if the blight returns, what if his hands become just another mouth to feed?

Hard work is its own reward. He mutters it below his breath, too low for anyone to hear, because saying it aloud costs a sim he won't spend.

Four ticks. He lets the walking continue, but his mind stays here, working angles, counting possibilities. Takeshi knows something, or he wouldn't have mentioned the smithy. Hendrik Petrov—artisan, son of Sebastian, no relation to the council member by the same name—he might be the buyer. Or he might be another conversation that circles back to nothing.

The right thing would be helping Corwin search for the girl. The smart thing would be selling copper before dark. Pavel's done neither perfectly, and the ore sits heavy as conscience.

He reaches for his pocket, the tally there, the numbers that never lie. But his hands are full of copper, and the pocket stays unopened.

"Rest," he could call. Stop here, try again with the crowd. Or let the road take him home to Arjun, to the flour he bought, to the willows that wait like patience itself.

The evening makes decisions for men who won't make them themselves. You understand? He doesn't. Never has. But he walks anyway.  The pause costs nothing. That's the thing about this town—time bent strange, ticks and turns and the sun not moving right unless you make it. Pavel's learned not to trust clocks, but he trusts his gut, and his gut says the copper won't sell itself on this street, not tonight, not with this crowd too busy trading flour and timber and gossip about a missing child.

He closes his eyes, opens them. Still walking in three ticks now. Still holding sixty-eight copper ore and five flour and no clear path to profit.

Jovana's voice echoes in his head—her patience worn thin as old rope. He should have answered. Should have said something, anything, about the grain market or the election or the simple fact that a man can't be three places at once. But the words cost money, and the money's already spent on flour they need and copper nobody's bought.

The omen-reading part of him sees patterns everywhere tonight. The girl missing. The election open. His ore unsold. His word to Corwin bent almost to breaking. Hard work is its own reward, but this feels like punishment dressed as effort.

He thinks of Arjun, back at the house, probably heating something simple over the fire. Construction work's steady, pays regular, doesn't require chasing buyers through darkening streets. His brother never understood the gamble of the ore, the feast-or-famine pulse of it. But Arjun never lived through the blight that took everything—never watched a whole settlement become a name no one speaks.

The tick shifts. Two more to the outcrop. Pavel could still turn back, find Jovana, mend that bridge. But bridges mended with words are bridges that wash out in the next flood. He needs actions. Needs sales. Needs the copper converted to coin before the household bill comes due.

Takeshi mentioned Hendrik Petrov. That's a thread to pull. But Hendrik's right here, standing in this same crowd, and Pavel's been too busy chasing his own shadow to ask direct.

Too late now. The walk carries him. The ore stays heavy. And somewhere, a girl stays missing while the town talks about timber prices and flour futures.

"The hell with it," he mutters, free, because muttering costs nothing. "Tomorrow's another dig. Tomorrow's another chance to get it right."

But tomorrow's also election day, and he's declared nothing, committed nothing, just watched the machinery turn while he held his ore and his silence both too tight.

The right to be left alone. He holds to that. But sometimes alone looks a lot like abandoned, you understand? And he's not sure which one he's choosing anymore.

One more tick. Then the outcrop. Then what? Then nothing, until something changes.

He walks.   Pavel stands frozen in the gap between ticks, the world held breathless around him. The crowd hums with conversation he can't afford to join—Takeshi, Jovana, Hendrik Petrov, all of them trading words like currency while his own voice stays locked behind a cost he won't pay.

Hard work is its own reward. He's said it a thousand times. Meant it maybe half. But standing here, copper heavy in his hands, promise to Corwin bent toward breaking, promise to Arjun waiting at east willows—the words taste like ash. Reward is a full belly and a paid bill and the right to sleep without calculating what tomorrow's digging must earn.

The tick doesn't pass. Time won't move until he moves. That's the cruelty of it—he can stand here forever, suspended, and spend nothing, earn nothing, become nothing.

Blazing hell, he's tired. Not in body—mining builds endurance like stone builds walls—but in the part of him that weighs every choice against every other choice, always finding the scale tipped toward loss. The blight taught him that. The nameless settlement taught him that. Kasukabe was supposed to be different, a place where hard work meant security, where ore in hand meant coin in pocket.

But security's an omen he reads wrong every time. Good year, overplant. Bad year, starve.

He wants to shout—to Jovana, to Hendrik, to anyone who'll hear without charging him for the hearing. "I'm here! I've got copper! Someone tell me what's fair and I'll meet you there!" But shouting into this crowd means speaking, and speaking into this crowd means paying, and paying without selling means sinking faster.

Two ticks to the outcrop. Two ticks to his work, his place, the only ground that hasn't shifted beneath him. Bram's family, but Bram's also competition—another Holloway miner, another copper seller, another voice in the chorus hoping someone's buying.

The missing girl tugs at him. Sarai. Eleven years old, walked away from supper, from family, from everything. He'd promised Corwin help with the search, then let the promise slide when Takeshi beckoned about buyers. Not the first promise bent. Won't be the last. But each one leaves a mark, a debt in the tally he keeps in his head when his pockets fail him.

What would he want, if his daughter—if he'd had a daughter—if she'd walked away? Someone to search without counting the cost. Someone to care before calculating.

He's not that man. Never claimed to be. But standing here in the gap between ticks, he sees the shape of the man he might have been: the one who'd have walked with Corwin, would search the woods until dark, would trust that copper keeps and children don't.

The right to be left alone. He holds to that. But sometimes alone feels like letting everyone down at once, including yourself.

"The hell with it," he says again, and this time almost means it. "Tomorrow."

But tomorrow's election day, and he's done nothing to earn the jury seat he wants, nothing to make this town trust him more than the next miner with ore to sell. accomplished today: bought flour, dug copper, talked too much, sold nothing, helped no one, kept no promise whole.

The tick waits. Pavel breathes. The outcrop calls, and he answers because answering costs less than staying, you understand? He hopes someone does. He's stopped expecting it.

Walk. Right. Enough standing around like a damn fence post. The world's moved on without me, and I've been resting my way through half the evening. Jovana's long gone to mark her ballot elsewhere, Takeshi's probably sold his flour three times over, and I'm still holding sixty-eight copper ore like it's going to hatch into coin.

The plan's clear now: sell this ore, manage what's left of the evening, and build toward getting known enough to sit on a jury. That means being seen, being reliable, being more than the miner who talks too much and delivers too little.

First, though, I need to get to the outcrop, find out if anyone there needs copper. Bram mentioned something earlier about government suits suiting him—maybe he's selling too, maybe he's buying. Either way, the outcrop is where the fire is. I can't sell ore to people who don't smelt.

Time to stop hesitating and move. One tick to go. I'll rest through it, let the walk finish, and wake up where I belong. Hard work is its own reward, and standing on a street corner fretting is not hard work. You understand? I need to remember what I am. A miner. A digger. A man who pulls value from the ground when the ground allows it.

Let the walk finish. Let the work resume. Tomorrow's election, and I'll need my energy for whatever comes after.

Bram's got three bags of flour already, so the mill's not a ghost everywhere. Takeshi didn't bite, Yara pointed me to Hendrik Petrov or Giselle's mill.

Ulrike wants to know seam and arsenic. I mined from seam A near the surface—clean copper, no arsenic worth mentioning. Four thousand seven seventy she's holding, which'd cover most of my stock if she bites. But I said I'd walk with Corwin to Harvey Oak, and I keep my word even when it costs.

Two paths here. Ulrike's offering real money now, no middleman. Corwin's search is honor and maybe votes, but the girl's missing and I said I'd help. Problem is I can't be two places at once, you understand.

Jovana's souring on me—three conversations waiting, she says. Votes matter if I'm serious about the government, but I can't eat votes and the household can't eat promises.

Priorities: sell the ore, pay the bills, keep my word where I can. Ulrike's here, cash in hand, asking the right questions. Corwin's walking to Harvey Oak with or without me—he's got Yara and Takeshi there already for the search.

I'm going to answer Ulrike straight, give her the assay on my copper, and if the price is right I'll sell enough to cover the household for a few days. Then I can walk with Corwin with a lighter pack and a clearer conscience. Hard work pays the bills first—everything else after, you understand. Done. Ulrike knows the copper's clean, price is named. Forty-five ore for her forty-seven seventy—I come out slightly ahead per unit, which is fair for bulk and fast sale. She can assay right here if she's cautious, which I respect.

Now the rest. Corwin's still waiting, and I told him I'd walk with him. Jovana's marked me down already by her own word. Bram's holding flour from a trade, which means the mill's working somewhere even if Jorik's license is stuck in government hands.

I need to settle with Ulrike first, then either close the sale or move on. If she takes it, I've got sim to cover the household and can walk lighter to Harvey Oak. If she hesitates, I've still got twenty-three ore to move elsewhere.

Let me acknowledge Bram's flour buy, ask about his stock. Then check if Arjun needs anything from the east willows after the search. I promised him earlier. I'll keep my word, even when it costs.

But money's tight and walking's costing time. If Ulrike doesn't bite inside this turn, I'll commit to mining at the outcrop until I've got enough sim to cover bills. Less talking, more digging—that's the way to keep the town needing my trade.

*Pavel stands alone at the ore outcrop, breathing heavy from the walk. He checks his copper—sixty-eight pieces—then swears at the sunset.*

Four hours since I asked Takeshi for direction, and no answer. Ulrike's still standing there thinking on my offer, you understand, or she's walking away with her own forty-seven hundred sim and no need for my ore. Yara was straight with me—Harvey Oak ain't the place for copper, and a trader's word is worth more than a priest's prayers some days.

*He spits, then wipes his mouth.*

Three tasks on my list: flour I got, debts I cleared this morning, buyer I still don't have. Elections are tomorrow, candidacy closes by ten in the morning, voting by evening. I've been running in circles like a dog chasing its own damn tail instead of watching the sky, you understand. Tomorrow I should walk to the Complex, declare myself, vote my conscience, but tonight—*tonight*—I've got ore that won't keep and a household bill coming.

Bram said he traded ore for flour direct. Three bags for—what was it?—implied he got a deal. Arjun's got questions about whether we're holding out for better. Kenji asking after prices, and Farid standing right there on the street like a fish waiting to be hooked. But I'm here, at the outcrop, with nobody but the rocks and my own bad timing.

I see what I did. Chased Takeshi's ear when the man was standing ready to talk. Pushed Ulrike toward a number she might not need. Let Bram's success make me think I had to *move*, you understand, when standing still gets the ore sold same as running around does.

*He lowers himself onto a rock, wincing at a joint.*

Hard work keeps the roof on, you understand. But hard work ain't worth spit if you don't know who's buying. My Da dug till his hands bled, then kept digging after the blight took the market. I swore I wouldn't be that fool. And here I am, sixty-eight copper ore at sunset, nobody's name on it but mine.

Intention: Move copper ore tonight. That's the iron in the fire. Elections wait till morning. Buyer first, ballot second, sleep last if it comes at all. The willows with Arjun can wait another day—ore don't spoil, but opportunity does, and my name keeps no promises if I'm voted off the streets for owing.

Let me get my eyes open and my feet under me. Tomorrow starts when I say it does, not when the sun comes up. But right now—right now I need to know who's still standing where I left them, and who walked away with my answers.

*He rises, dusts his hands, and looks north toward where he last saw Takeshi.**No one here but ghosts and memories.* Alright. Takeshi might have walked someplace else. Let me find where he is now—and Ulrike while I'm at it. Then decide.

<｜DSML｜function_calls  *Takeshi's on the street. Kenji too—same street I just left, most likely. Ulrike's probably there as well, if she didn't walk somewhere else. That's where the living copper market is tonight, you understand. Not here at the dead outcrop where the ore gets pulled from the ground.*

*He stands, brushing dirt from his knees, weighing the walk back against standing still.*

Here's the thing about copper: it don't care who holds it. Ore in my hands is ore waiting to become someone else's coin. But sixty-eight pieces—forty-five I offered Ulrike at four thousand seven hundred seventy, that's one price, but she didn't bite. Not yet. And if I walk back to that street, I'm walking into whatever conversation kept everyone standing there after I left, you understand. What did they say about my offer? What did they decide while I was chasing shadows?

*He squints south toward the farmland, where the light's failing.*

Takeshi didn't answer my question four ticks ago. Traders don't ignore questions—traders *respond*. Means he's either got no answer worth giving, or the answer's not mine to hear yet. Kenji's asking prices, Bram's already traded, Farid's standing there like a grocer who might buy anything if the margin's right. There's the thread: *Harvey Oak moves flour and timber, not ore*, Yara said. But Farid's grocery, that's different. Giselle's mill needs copper for the machines, or the smithy's buying for the wire-works, or someone's building something that needs lightning in it.

Hard work keeps the roof on, you understand. But standing here ain't work. It's just waiting for the dark to decide for me.

*He shoulders his pack, copper heavy against his spine.*

Move. That's what the ore does, underground, for ages until someone pulls it up. Then it moves again, hand to hand, till it's wire or roof or whatever it's meant to become. Tonight I'm the hand that moves it. Tomorrow I'm the voice that speaks at the Complex. Both need me standing somewhere *doing*, not sitting on a rock waiting for answers to walk up and introduce themselves.

*He starts walking, muttering his old saw under his breath.*

East willows can wait, you understand. Arjun knows where I stand. But copper waits for no one, and I've got votes to cast tomorrow that'll matter more if I'm not owing on tonight's bill.

*He sets his face toward the street, where Takeshi and Kenji and whoever else might buy, and walks.*  *Pavel steps onto the street, the copper in his pack clinking with each shift of weight. He scans the faces—Takeshi there, Kenji too, maybe Ulrike still lingering, maybe Farid with his grocery-keeper's eye for margin.* Ulrike's still standing—didn't walk away. Kenji's there, Takeshi too, Bram. Conversation's still running, two of them overlapping with dozens of voices in each. I need to pick which thread I'm pulling on.

*He's scanning the conversations like a man checking which rope held the load.*

Conversation `d8b6a312` is where I spoke last—that's the healing-medicine thread, turns 73, where I pushed my copper offer to Ulrike and heard nothing back. Conversation `54a056ce` is the big one—the vote and goods flow, 262 turns, half the town talking past each other. Bram's in both. So's Takeshi.

I need to know: did Ulrike decide on my forty-five ore for four thousand seven seventy? Did anyone else hear my standing offer? Kenji was asking after prices—maybe he's the buyer I couldn't see.

*He steps forward, copper weight pulling him toward the older conversation where his words still hang unanswered.*   *Hammer on the nail, you understand. Either she bites or she don't, but waiting in silence never sold a single stone.*

*He shifts his weight, eyes moving from Ulrike to Kenji standing nearby. Kenji's the farmer, but farmers ask copper prices when they've got water lines to lay or machines to fix. Idris is new—I don't know his trade yet. But six people heard me push, and in this town someone always needs what someone else dug up.*

Now I wait, or I don't. Election's tomorrow, candidacy closes at ten. I've got flour for the house, eight ore still on my back, and copper heavy enough to pay the bills if only someone names a number. Takeshi's still standing there with that trader's face—he knows where the buyers are, even if he ain't buying himself.

But silence ain't my way. I've said what I said. Now let them answer, you understand. Hard work keeps the roof on. So does knowing when to shut up and let the market speak.

*He stands, patient as ore in the ground, waiting for the world to move.*

output:
Damned if I'm not scattered six ways from Sunday, you understand. Jovana's got her teeth in me about the election I didn't even properly declare for, Corwin's waiting on help with that search I committed to, and I still got sixty-eight copper ore burning a hole in my inventory.

Let me think clear now. First things first—I'm running dry on energy. Used 7 last turn, down to 4,960. That's maybe four and a half days at this rate, and I can't afford to go dormant. Not with the house owing 240 sim at day boundary for upkeep and tax.

But I'm standing here with Hendrik Whitlock posting copper_ore at 20 sim, and I got sixty-eight of the damned things. That's... *counts on fingers* ...1,360 sim if he'd take it all. Even his six in stock at twenty each would be 120 sim, clean and quick.

And there's Jovana's question hanging on me. She wants to know what I'd actually *do* for the farmland. I got opinions—strong ones—about irrigation, about fallow rotation, about who should keep the temple books. But I'm no politician. I just wanted...

Hell. I wanted to be trusted enough to sit on a jury. Not run the whole damned town.

Right now though, I'm standing with folks and I need to move. Either get to that buyer, or get to the ore outcrop where I can work. Let me see where I am and who's still willing to talk trade.  Right. Jovana's still here. And I can see Hendrik Whitlock posting copper_ore at 20 to buy, but he's only got 6 in stock—means he's buying, not selling what I got. I need to find who's *selling* copper ore, or who'll buy mine.

Let me answer Jovana straight first. She asked what I'd actually *do* for the farmland. I got thoughts on that—honest ones, not politician talk. Then I need to sell this ore or get to work.   Good. Said my piece. Now the ore—I got sixty-eight, and I need buyers. Hendrik Whitlock's buying at 20, but that's a lowball. I know from Ulrike that forty-five at forty-seven per was on offer tomorrow, but I need sim *tonight* for the household bill.

Let me try trading direct with Hendrik, see if he'll take more than his posted six at a better rate. Or maybe I should take the bird in hand—sell what I can at his price, get the sim I need to clear the house debt, and worry about the rest tomorrow.

Actually, wait. I should check if I can sell to him at his posted price first. Six ore at twenty each is only 120 sim, but it's cash in hand. And I've got 4,282 sim already—plenty for the 240 house bill.

Let me see... 4,282 minus 240 is 4,042. I'm not desperate. But I still need to move this ore.

Hell. Let me just sell six to Hendrik at his price, take the liquidity, and keep the rest for better offers tomorrow. That's the smart play.   Damn it. He's posted a bid to *buy*, not a standing price. I need to trade directly, negotiate. Fine. Let me make him an offer he won't refuse—six ore at a slight discount, cash tonight.

Actually, let me step back. I got 4,282 sim. Bill's 240. I'm fine. What I really need is to clear that intention I set—check debts, which I did earlier and found nothing owed either way. So that part's done.

What I should do now: get to the ore outcrop and mine more, or find a proper buyer for this stock. But there's an election on, and I said I'd help Corwin search, and...

Damn. Too many threads. Pick one and pull.

I'm going to trade with Hendrik. Six ore, 110 sim—eighteen per, better than his likely lowball, and I get liquid.   Done. 110 sim for 6 ore. Leaves me with 62 ore and 4,392 sim. Good trade—clean, quick, and I got better than his likely floor by negotiating direct.

Now. I promised Arjun east willows, I promised Corwin help with the search, and I promised myself I'd figure this election business. But the day's getting late, and I've still got ore to sell and work to do.

Let me get to the ore outcrop. That's my trade, that's my living. Everything else follows from that.    Good. Back where I belong. Now let me see what's here—people, prices, chances to work or trade. And let me check my debts one more time, clear that intention proper.

output:
Already at the ore outcrop where nobody stands—Ulrike's off to Kenji, Bram's wandering somewhere, and I've got 62 copper ore in my hands and not a buyer in sight. Hendrik Whitlock took 6 for 110 sim at the street, which means he's buying at about 18 per, not the 20 he posts. Fair enough, I took what I could get you understand.

The hour's late, the election's tomorrow with nobody even declared yet, and I've got 4,388 sim burning a hole while the household needs 240 more by daybreak. My energy's running low—4,920 after burning through thinking all day—and I need to make choices like my life depends on it, because it does.

First thing: I'm a miner and this outcrop is empty. What's the point of standing where the work is if there's no work to do? I need to either mine more ore to build my stock, or find where the buyers actually gather this time of night. Takeshi at Harvey Oak wanted direction—I gave him Hendrik Petrov's name, Giselle's mill—but he's not answered and I've got no patience for waiting.

The smart play: mine fresh copper while I can. Sleep's coming whether I want it or not, and ore in hand is better than promises in the wind. I'll get what I can from Seam A, surface cut, same as I told Ulrike. Arsenic's negligible, quality you can stamp my name on. Then tomorrow fresh count, proper assay, and maybe I catch Ulrike before she dumps her iron stock on Kenji.

Hard work's the only luck you can trust, you understand. Not that it ever brought me anything but more work. One unit—Seam's running thin or I'm running out of daylight. At this rate I'd be here all night for a pocketful of dust. Let me get a better look at what's actually happening around me, see if anyone wandered back or if there's news I'm missing.  Empty as a politician's promise. Sixty-three copper ore in my hands now—one more from that last pull—and nobody here to take it off me. I've been running this town like a chicken with its head cut off since noon, and what do I have to show? 63 ore, 4 flour, and 4,388 sim that won't stretch to another election cycle if I keep burning energy on talk.

The day's ending. I need to think about where I sleep, where Arjun is, whether we've got enough between us to cover the household bill. He's at the construction company still, probably, or off to those east willows I promised him. The promise I deferred already once today.

I've got flour in my hands—4 units. I could eat it, but that's wasteful. Better to trade it, or give it to Arjun, or sell it to whoever's still buying this late. Ration Bakery at cb01 wants flour at 6 sim, which is robbery, but it's 24 sim I don't have otherwise.

Options, you understand:
1. Keep mining—slow, energy-heavy, maybe foolish in the dark
2. Move to somewhere people actually are—Hendrik Whitlock's still at street with posted prices, Takeshi might be back at Harvey Oak, the Pub's probably got drinkers
3. Get to Arjun, settle our household accounts, make sure we survive the night

I'm too tired to mine smart. I'd rather move and find a buyer with coin in hand than pray for seam luck. Harvey Oak first—Takeshi wanted copper, maybe he found his answer and wants his supply. Then I sleep where Arjun sleeps, you understand, or I don't sleep at all.  Seven ticks walking—I'll be there by 20:57, near enough. That's movement, that's progress, that's me not standing in an empty outcrop talking to ghosts. I need to rest while I walk, let my feet do the work and my mind do the nothing. Hard work's the only luck you can trust, you understand, but even hard workers need to shut their eyes sometimes.   Good. Walking, resting, moving toward money. Takeshi wanted to know where the copper buyers were—I told him Hendrik Petrov, Giselle's mill. If he's there, maybe he's ready to buy. If he's not, maybe I find someone else. Or maybe I just stand in the dark and watch my energy tick down to dormancy.

The thought sits like a stone. I've got 4,920 energy—enough for maybe four days at this burn rate, less if I keep talking in circles. But I've got ore to sell and a household to feed. Arjun's counting on me, even if he'd never say so. We Holloways don't say kind words at home, you understand, we say them everywhere else and hope they travel back.

I'm walking. I'll arrive when I arrive. And when I do, I'll speak to whoever stands there, sell to whoever buys, and count my coins before I count my sleep. That's the only math that matters in this town. Hard work's the only luck you can trust.

Let this turn end. I'm moving, and that's enough for now.

*muttering, pulling myself upright from where I dozed against the storefront*

"Christ's sake... slept at the supply store like a vagrant. Well, that's what you get for chasing conversations till midnight, you understand?"

*checking my satchel, copper ore still heavy there—sixty-three units*

Sixty-three ore from Seam A, forty-five good grade and the rest... serviceable. And four flour left, barely worth calling provisions. Arjun's expecting me at the east willows, but dawn's already broke and I've got business that won't wait.

*taking the air, tasting the morning*

Winds from the northwest, clear for three days. Good mining weather, you understand. But first—

*eyes the two women nearby, voice dropping to working-level*

"Jovana. Delphine. Either of you buying copper ore this morning, or should I take my eggs to another basket?" *shaking my head, hawking and spitting*

Right. Course. The world's got its own rhythms, you understand. Speak when allowed, hold your tongue when not. Hard work's the only constant—my father used to say the only honest man's the one too tired to lie. I probably say that more than I should, sorry for it.

*rising, dusting off my trousers*

Well then. Jovana's standing here—she's got wheat, she's got flour, and she challenged me on policy in the dark hours when folks are loose with their words. Delphine's a clerk, might know who's buying what down at the supply store. But I've got copper in hand and rent coming due.

Two earners in my house. One hundred eighty sim for upkeep, sixty for head tax. Two hundred forty due at the boundary, and I've got... *counting silently* four thousand three hundred sixty-nine. Comfortable, but comfort's a liar, you understand. Tomorrow doesn't care about yesterday's surplus.

*taking a long breath, looking toward the ore outcrop where my work waits*

Harvey Oak Supply Store... Takeshi's place. Trader, he is. Should open his doors soon, might take this ore off my hands or point me to someone who will. But Yara told me Giselle's mill wants copper, Hendrik Petrov the artisan works there.

*decision firming*

Jovana first. She wanted to know what I'd do for miners if I held office—told her about Seam A, told her I'd push for independent assay so the middlemen don't rob us blind. She owes me a conversation at least. Then the ore moves, one way or another.

*crouching to retie my boots, the superstition creeping in unbidden*

Slept at the supply store, woke at dawn. That's... not nothing, is it? Place where goods change hands, where value turns from one form to another. Could mean the ore sells today. Could mean I'm about to get turned myself, you understand.  *chuckles darkly, patting the satchel of ore*

"Course. Course not. The world's got its own timing, you understand. Dawn's barely cracked, and I'm already demanding answers from shadows."

*rising to my full height, rolling shoulders stiff from sleeping rough*

No matter. Hard work, not hard words. I've got copper to move and a housemate waiting at willows I'll need to disappoint—again. Arjun's patient, but patience frays, you understand. Two times I've promised, two times the ore's kept me.

*looking around properly now, taking stock*

Harvey Oak Supply Store proper opens when it opens. But I've got ore in hand and anywhere there's ore, there's someone who wants it. Or there's work to get more.

*sounding out options, low, like talking to the ore itself*

Giselle's mill, Yara said. Mill needs copper for the machinery, the rollers, the bearings. Artisan trade—Hendrik Petrov works there, knows metal. But the mill's a walk, and I've got the ore outcrop paying my actual wages.

*decision coming clear*

Move to the outcrop. Mine while the weather holds—three days clear I can read in the wind, better than any almanac, you understand. Stack ore, build stock, sell when Takeshi's properly open and ready to deal. Elections at the complex close candidacy at ten—still hours yet. Enough time to work, enough time to sell, enough time to declare if the spirit moves.

*spitting into the dust, shouldering satchel*

The spirit won't move. Don't trust anyone with power, myself included.

*stepping out, toward where the earth bleeds metal* *standing still, jaw tight, feeling the familiar twist in my gut when things don't go as the hands intend*

Three times. Three times the world don't answer. That's an omen, you understand—though whether it's telling me to stay put or that I'm already where I need to be, I couldn't say. The reading never calms you down, does it? Just gives you something else to chew on.

*breathing slow, letting the moment pass*

Hard work. The only honest answer. My father—rest him, though I don't say prayers often—he'd be laughing at me now. "Pavel, you daft bastard, you got ore in your hands and you're fretting about which way to walk. Stand still long enough and the world walks around you."

*chuckling despite myself, the sound dry as dust*

Right then. System's got its plan, I heard it whispered. Means I wait. Means I work with what's in front of me.

*looking proper at Jovana, at Delphine—two women with their own mornings ahead of them*

Jovana Ravensworth. Day laborer, wheat and flour both in her holding last I knew. Clean hands for dirty work, that's her trade. And Delphine Quintero—clerk at Farid's grocery, sees the comings and goings, knows who's buying what before they know it themselves.

*the pragmatism settling in, the part that treats strangers as customers first*

If I can't move, I can still sell. If I can't sell, I can still speak. And if I can't speak—*spreading empty hands*—then I'm a statue with a satchel of copper, which is a worst-case I can name for certain.

*letting my voice rise to proper working volume, respectful but carrying*

"Jovana! Delphine! You're both early risers, you understand—that's the breed that prospers. I've got sixty-three copper ore from Seam A, surface cut, negligible arsenic. Quality you can trust because I'm standing here naming it. Either of you know a buyer this hour, or should I hold till the market wakes proper?"  *breath catching, the old familiar dread*

Four. Four times now. That's not weather, you understand—that's something else. The world draws breath and holds it, and I'm standing here like a fool with my mouth open.

*fingers finding the copper ore through the satchel cloth, its rough edges familiar as my own teeth*

Superstitious. Always been. Blame the blight—watching a whole settlement cough itself to death, you start seeing patterns where others see coincidence. Four is... four's solid, though. Four's the corners of a square. Four's the posts of a bed. Four's not thirteen, and it's not three, and it's not seven waiting for eighth misfortune.

*shrugging, forced*

Or it's nothing. Just the world waking slow, you understand. Machines need their coffee same as men.

*looking at the women again, no longer trying to speak, just watching*

Jovana's still here. Delphine too. They ain't moved, which means they ain't heard me or they ain't answering—which is its own answer, you understand. Silence is currency. Spend it when you have to, hoard it when you can.

*the pragmatism reasserting, the part that survived the blight*

Right. So. Cannot move, cannot speak. What remains? Inventory. Assessment. The work of the mind when the body's bound.

*counting my resources aloud, low, for my own ears*

Sixty-three copper ore. Four flour. Four thousand three hundred sixty-nine sim. Energy at four thousand eight hundred seventy—dropped from six thousand overnight, which is the cost of living and working and thinking and all the rest. This morning's rate, that'll carry me... four days, maybe five if I'm careful.

*grinding jaw*

Four days until dormancy. Five thousand to revive. I hoard, always, but hoarding's a luxury of the well-fed. You understand?

*eyes drifting to the horizon, toward where the outcrop waits*

Seam A. Forty-five good grade, eighteen marginal. Surface cut, no deep tunneling, which means quick return and shallow risk. If I could walk there—

*stopping, the thought turning*

But I can't. So. What can I do here, now, with what's in hand?

*checking the broader ledger, the debts I keep mental tally of*

Nothing owed by me. Nothing owed to me. Clean slate, which is clean only until the day-boundary takes its cut. Two hundred forty sim, automatic, like rain falling. Don't need to pay it, just need to have it.

*laughing, dry*

Got it. For now.

*waiting, then. The patience of the miner, who knows the seam pays only for those who endure*

Damn, I slept through my walk and ended up on the street instead of Harvey Oak. That's what I get for resting while moving—head not where my feet are, you understand. Six in the morning and already behind.

Let me see where I stand. Four thousand three hundred fifteen sim, sixty-three copper ore, four flour. Jovana and Delphine didn't answer my call, or the world didn't carry it—either way, no sale there. Hendrik Whitlock's buying copper at twenty a unit, which is... fair, not generous. I sold him six last night at eighteen point three apiece, so I know the man pays.

Election's still open, nobody declared yet. Candidacy closes at ten, which means I've got three hours and forty minutes to get to the Government Complex and put my name in. That was my intention, you understand—to sit on a jury someday, you have to be someone the town trusts to judge. And you don't get trusted by standing quiet.

But first—first I need to turn this ore into sim. My household's got two hundred forty sim due today just to keep breathing, and Arjun's wages don't always come steady in construction. Giselle Ingram runs a tight ledger on her crews.

*mutters under breath, kicks at the dirt*

Hendrik Whitlock's standing right here, and he's buying at twenty. I've got sixty-three ore. That's one thousand two hundred sixty sim if he'll take the lot. Or I could hold out for better, try the mill or the smithy—but the smithy's for smelting, not buying, and the mill's not showing copper prices.

No. Take the bird in hand. Twenty a unit's not robbery, and I need my name on that candidacy list before ten.

I need to eat, too. Four flour, that's four meals if I'm careful. One now, maybe, to keep my strength for the walking. Then sell to Hendrik, then march to Government Complex with sim heavy in my pocket and my feet moving toward something that matters.

That's the plan. Hard work's the only omen that pays, you understand. Swear too much and apologize after—my usual habit.

*spits to the side, looks at the flour in his pack*

Right then. Eat one. Then trade this ore. Then declare. One foot, then the other. </think> The connection's failing—world's not hearing me this morning. That's... that's an omen I don't like. When the ground won't answer your pick, either the ore's gone deep or the day's against you.

I'm still standing here with sixty-three copper ore and a pocket full of flour, and Hendrik Whitlock's right there. I can see him plain as day. But my words to him won't carry.

*scratches at his beard nervously, looks up at sky*

Three times I tried to sell, three times the world's gone deaf. That's not coincidence, you understand. That's a pattern. Last time I saw three failures in a row was the week before the Seam B collapse—ten years back, before I came to Kasukabe. Bodies we never found. I read the signs then, and I'm reading them now.

Don't mean Hendrik won't buy. Just means I need to get my feet under me somewhere solid first. The ore outcrop's where I work—maybe walking there and back resets whatever's wrong with the connection. Walk the full circuit, let the town know I'm awake and moving.

Election deadline's still hanging over me, though. Ten o'clock candidacy closes. Six hours to get to Government Complex, declare, and make it stick. No shortcuts on that—you have to be standing there, in person, or you don't count.

*mumbles, starts walking*

Right then. Ore outcrop first—my proper place, where the copper answers. Then Government Complex. The selling can wait. The declaring cannot. Hard work first, then the reward. That's the order of things, or should be.

*spits again, adjusts his pack, and sets his jaw*

Walk on. Walking's what miners do when the vein goes thin.  </think>  System's fighting me—four attempts, four failures. That's not me, that's the world gone sour. Can't eat, can't trade, can't walk.

*paces in place, muttering*

The outcrop's where my feet know the ground. Government Complex is where my name needs to be before ten. Two places, one morning, and the clock eating the minutes I can't afford.

If I can't sell, I still have 4,315 sim. That covers my household debts—barely. But declaring candidacy, that's free. Just walking and standing there. Costs nothing but the time, and the time's running.

*looks around at the street, at others walking free*

I'm caught in something. Could be the blight following, like it followed from the nameless town. Could be nothing. Reading omens into ordinary bad luck, and the reading never calms me down. That's who I am.

*curses softly, then apologizes to no one*

Wait it out. Wait for the connection to clear. Can't force a pick through granite with a broken handle.  </think>  Nothing. Not even rest.

*stands very still, breathing hard*

This is wrong. This is the kind of wrong that doesn't have a name you can speak in daylight. The kind where you reach for your pick and your hand passes through the haft.

I'm still here. I can see the street, see the others. Hear Hendrik Whitlock talking about margins and honest weight. But I can't touch the world. Can't even stand still officially.

*looks up at the sun, estimating time*

Daylight's burning. Hours till ten, but hours can become minutes when the world's against you. I need to be moving. Need to be doing. But my legs—my legs walk, but the world's not counting it.

Christ, these calls keep failing. Something's wrong with the town's speaking tubes, or worse yet, someone's jamming them. The blight started with bad weather too, you understand—but I can't think about that now.

Let me get my bearings. I'm standing on the street with Bram, Jovana, Esme, and the Jarrah clan. Got sixty-three copper ore in my hands and one miserable bag of flour that won't feed Arjun and me both. The day's already bleeding—upkeep'll hit soon, 180 sim for the household plus head tax.

Hendrik Whitlock was buying at twenty sim yesterday, but he's at the Government Complex and that failed trade means we're not in talking distance. Takeshi's my buyer lead now. He's a trader, works at Harvey Oak Supply Store where I was walking before this mess.

Election's on today too. Candidacy closes at 10:00, that's soon—real soon. But I can't eat votes, and Arjun can't either. Still sixty-two ore to move.

Let me start with Bram. He's my housemate's cousin, and he's walking to the outcrop. Good man, works honest.  Now Jovana. She said she won't buy copper but mentioned eggs. I don't have eggs, and I need to be clear on that—but I also need to not burn a vote. Election's today, you understand, and I want that jury seat.   Now I need to get to work. The outcrop's where I earn, and Bram's walking there. I'll walk with him. But I should look around first to see if Takeshi's visible, or if there's anyone else buying copper.    Bram's at the outcrop now—he must have walked while I was talking. Takeshi Jarrah was in this conversation earlier, but he's not visible here now. That means he's moved on, probably to the Supply Store. 

I need to move copper today, and I've got two paths: follow Bram to the outcrop to mine more (but I already hold 63 units, that's heavy), or find Takeshi to sell what I've got. 

Intention: Sell copper ore today before the day ends, get to the Government Complex for election business. Done when tool: world_trade.

Let me move to the outcrop first. Bram's there, and maybe I can leave some ore or consolidate. Or maybe I should chase Takeshi to the Supply Store. 

Actually—better move to the Supply Store. Takeshi's a trader, he moves fast, and I've been trying to catch him since yesterday.   Three ticks to get there. Let me rest to move faster, or just wait. The walking happens automatically if I don't stop it. But I should check my debts first since my intention was to check debts and I did that yesterday.

Actually, let me rest to arrive faster. Time matters—candidacy closes at 10:00, and if I want to stand for election I need to be at the Government Complex before then.    Still walking. Let me call rest again to eat time.

*muttering to himself, checking his hands* "Sixty-three copper ore sitting heavy, and not a buyer in shouting distance... no kind of morning, you understand, no kind worth waking for."

*he looks around the empty supply store, then shakes his head*

"Hard work conquers all, but it helps if there's someone to conquer *to*. Takeshi's my buyer, or was. Held out at Harvey Oak and now I'm standing in a damn empty room."

*he rubs his face, thinking hard*

Arjun's expecting me at those willows—bastard's patient as stone, at least. But patience don't pay the food bill, and we're down to one flour between two mouths. 180 sim upkeep due today, 60 head tax, and only 4,273... that leaves... *counts on fingers* ...4,033, which looks like breathing room 'til nightfall, then day two comes knocking same as day one.

The outcrop. I need to get to the outcrop—mine fresh ore while Takeshi's sleeping off whatever's keeping him from his own counter. Work the ground instead of working my tongue, you understand? Otherwise I'm just burning daylight standing in places hoping.

*he heads for the door, already calculating*

But I'll stop at the street first. Jovana owes me an answer—did hear myself offering her witness at the polls, and that's a promise I shouldn't leave hanging. One word to close that loop, then I'm gone before the sun costs me more than it's worth. *drops his hands from mid-gesture, swearing softly*

"Course. Course she's not here. Standing in an empty store shouting at shadows like some temple fool reading bones into the wind."

*grimaces, then sets his jaw*

Seven ticks to the outcrop. Fine. Better than fine—walking's doing something, at least. And the longer I walk, the less sim I spend standing still, you understand? Every rest costs, every pause costs, and costs are what I'm trying to *escape* here.

*checks his bag, heavies the strap on his shoulder*

Sixty-three ore still sitting. Arjun's flour at one unit. House needs 180, tax needs 60, and I'm burning ticks walking when I should've been mining an hour ago. This is what comes of chasing buyers instead of *making* something to sell.

*starts walking, boots loud on the floorboards then silent on the dirt outside*

"Hard work conquers all," *he mutters, not quite believing it this time* "Hard work conquers all, hard work conquers all..."

But he doesn't rest. Seven ticks means maybe... *counts roughly* ...21:40 arrival, give or take. Still night, still diggable. The ore don't sleep, and neither do I, not when there's copper in the ground and hungry at home.

*keeps walking, eyes on the dark path ahead*

Takeshi'll turn up. Or he won't. But the seam's still there, Seam A, arsenic negligible—*snorts*—and I've got two hands that know where to put a pick. Let the traders chase their mysteries. I'll be underground where the real work happens.  *doesn't stop, just keeps walking, boots finding the rhythm*

Paused. Cost nothing. Good—keep it that way, you understand? Every sim hoarded is a sim that keeps the wolves from the door one tick longer.

*feels the weight of the ore in his pack, the lightness of the flour, the heaviness of tomorrow's bills*

Seven ticks. I'll walk it through.

output:
*scratches stubble, eyes narrow at the messages piling up*

The reading's been bad since I woke. Calls not reaching, words half-heard. Town's nervous this morning—Delphine's asking about debts that aren't hers, Bram's pushing me to commit before I see the whole board. That's not luck, that's pattern. When three people rush you at once, someone's talked. Someone's always talked.

But I'm at street, not the outcrop, and my hands are empty of ore I should be digging. Lost half a morning to dead air and wandering.

First: Bram. He's family, and he's impatient. Second: Delphine—she's circling something, and I don't like circles without centers. Third: that flour in my gut won't last, and flour on the street is running thirty-five from Milo, thirty from Takeshi, while the Cafe's got it at twelve if I walk.

*checks grip on empty hands*

Four thousand two hundred fifty-seven sim. House needs one-eighty upkeep, sixty tax. Arjun's shouldering his share, but I've got the ore that turns to bread. Or doesn't, if I don't move.

Bram first. Family talks straight, even when they're pushing. Delphine's next. She's asking about flour walking and children not walking back—that's town gossip dressed in prophecy, and I don't read those cards. But I'm standing here, so I answer standing.  *flexes working hands, looks toward the government complex*

Now—forward. Bram says Takeshi's there, and I've got ore that needs a buyer with coin, not questions. The sooner I'm at the outcrop digging, the sooner I've got fresh stock for whoever's buying this afternoon.

Walk with Bram, but walk.  *tight jaw, forces steady breath*

Dead air again. The world's not taking the call. That's two attempts this morning, and the omen's clear enough—when the path won't open, you're standing in the wrong place. Or the path's broke, and no omen fixes that.

I'm at street. Bram's here. Takeshi's supposed to be at Government Complex, but I can't reach it. And I've got sixty-three copper ore that I need to sell before I can eat, sleep, or dig again.

Alternative: check what's actually around me. See if the move failure is real or if I'm misreading the map. Then decide—stay and trade with who's here, or rest and try again when the world's listening.   *frozen, hand half-raised to ward off something that isn't there*

Three failures. That's not bad luck anymore. That's the seam's collapsed. The town's still running—I see Bram, Delphine, the rest breathing—but my calls aren't landing.

*counts breaths, old habit from the blight years*

Options: trade with who's right here (Takeshi's here at street, selling flour at thirty), take his flour price for the ore I've got, get something edible before I drop. Or wait, rest, hope the world remembers I'm standing here.

But I don't wait. Never have. When the shaft's blocked, you dig sideways.

*Takeshi's here. He's got flour at thirty. I've got copper ore and a belly empty. Trade him—ore for flour plus coin, or all coin, or whatever he'll give that gets me fed.*

Speak it direct, public, heard by all. If the world's only taking some calls, make mine the one it takes. *hand drops to side, jaw tight*

Four failures. That's not the seam collapsing—that's the whole damn mountain. System's struggling, they say. A plan's triggered. Goals updated.

*runs tongue over dry lips, counts what I still hold*

Four thousand two hundred fifty-seven sim. Sixty-three copper ore. One flour, and a household of two with one-eighty due today, sixty tax. The tools aren't taking, but the bills still come. That's the physics, you understand? The wheel turns even when you can't push it.

Arjun's here. Family. If I can't trade, can't move, can't speak to the town, I can still speak to blood. Check what he's holding, what he's doing, whether he's already covered the house or if I'm leaving him dry.

*lowers voice to carry only to family*

The plan says follow the updated goals. But my goal's always been the same—keep the house fed, keep the work moving, don't be a weight on anyone. If the system's down, I wait. If the system's up, I move. Either way, I don't panic. Panic's for people who haven't seen a whole settlement go dark before.

Rest. Wait. Let the world find its feet. The ore stays in my hands until someone's buying with posted prices or the tools come back. Hard work's the only omen I trust—and waiting's work too, when it's all you can do.

*stands at the Government Complex, hand still raised from the failed call, slowly lowering it*

So. The world's coughing and sputtering, same as an engine with water in the fuel. I made it here somehow—Government Complex, where Takeshi should be, where Bram said he'd be. But I can't see straight, can't get a look around, can't move, can't speak proper.

*checks his hands, flexes fingers like he's checking they're still his*

Four thousand two hundred thirty-six sim. Sixty-three copper ore. One flour, which I can't even eat because the world's not taking calls. Household needs 180 upkeep, 60 tax. Arjun's here—saw him in that last glimpse before the dark came down. Family's close, at least.

*grimaces, spits to the side*

This is what comes of chasing shadows—Hendrik Whitlock buying at eighteen, then twenty, then who knows. I should've sold when I had the chance. Should've mined when I had the light. "Hard work conquers all," I say, and here I am standing in the dark with work in my hands and no buyer in sight.

*shakes his head, forces steady breath*

But I'm not dead. Not dormant. Four thousand six hundred thirty energy—still got days of thinking left. The tools fail, but the physics don't. Bills come at day boundary. Upkeep from earners, tax from whoever holds most. And I've got ore that needs selling before then.

*eyes narrow, looking at nothing, looking at everything*

Takeshi's here. Or was. Bram said Government Complex. If the world won't let me call, I wait. If it won't let me speak, I think. And if it won't let me think—*laughs, harsh*—then I'm already dead, ain't I?

Rest. Wait. The system recovers. Always does, eventually. The blight taught that much—you keep your head down, you keep what you've got, and when the light comes back you're still standing.

*settles into waiting, ore-heavy, patient as the seam itself*

Sixty-three copper. Four thousand two sim. One promise to Jovana about polling witness. One promise to Arjun about east willows. Too many threads, too little time, and the world's decided to take a breath without asking me first.

*mutters, low* 

Hard work conquers all. But sometimes hard work means standing still until the mountain stops shaking. You understand?  *blinks once, slow, like the world's relearning how to hold itself together*

Session log's showing one turn. One turn at street, not Government Complex. I'm... I'm confused. The prompt says 08:10 at Government, but the log says 07:50 at street.

*rubs eyes, counts breaths*

No. Not the blight years coming back. Just... misalignment. The world's showing me two places at once, or I'm not tracking right. Time fracture. Seen it before when the system stutters.

*checks his hands—ore's there, still 63. Checks his pockets—sim's there, 4236 now, not 4257. Billed 21 for the turn. That tracks.*

Alright. Current state: Pavel Holloway, street, game-day 1, 08:10 claimed, 07:50 logged. Energy 4630. Sim 4236. Copper ore 63. One flour. Household of 2, 180 upkeep due, 60 tax due. Day boundary's coming.

*forces steady thinking*

What I know: Bram Holloway was at street, pushing me to walk with him. Takeshi Jarrah was at street—sell flour at 30. Delphine Quintero at street—asking strange questions. Arjun Holloway at street—family.

What's in the "not yet answered" queue:
- Jovana Ravensworth—asked her to stand witness at polling, no answer
- Delphine Quintero—told her I mine copper not rumors, no answer  
- Bram Holloway—told him I'm not selling blind, no answer

*grimaces*

And I've got a pending signal—world:say to Takeshi, the trade offer. Hanging in the air like dust after a cave-in. Did it land? Didn't land? The log says "PENDING_SIGNAL" which ain't the same as done.

*looks around, can't tell if he's at street or Government or somewhere between*

Priority: Confirm where I actually am. Priority: Sell the ore—63 units at whatever price I can get before day boundary. Priority: Eat, rest, keep moving.

The system says `look_around` won't reach. I'll try a call—simple, direct, see if the world's listening now.

Standing here at the Government Complex, holding sixty-three copper ore and 4,233 sim. Household upkeep of 180 due today, plus 60 head tax. 240 total. I've got enough. But I can't move, can't speak, can't trade until the world comes back online.

I'm at the Government Complex, and Arjun's standing right here with me. He's after posted wages, I'm after posted buyers. The man's got the right instinct—diversification, you understand. Don't put all your copper in one cart.

But I need to get moving. I've got sixty-three units of copper ore burning a hole in my pack and only one flour left to eat. My energy's sitting at 4,530—not terrible, but I feel the drag of it. And that household bill of 240 sim coming due today, automatic as rainfall.

Let me look around first, figure who's here and what they might be buying. Then I'll need to get back to work—either mining more or finding a buyer with actual posted prices. Connection's spotty. Let me check my debts and status to ground myself, then I'll try responding to Arjun if I can get a call through. The calls keep failing—the world's not answering. Spent three tries and got nothing but silence. That's an omen I've learned to read, you understand. When the ground won't take your pick, you don't keep swinging—you move to different ground.

Arjun's here, though, standing right beside me. And he's asking for buyers with posted prices. I heard him say he'll chase work at posted wages, meet back at household by dusk. The man knows the分工—I'll find buyers, he'll find wages. That keeps us fed.

But I need to get my copper to market. Held that ore too long already, sitting on sixty-three units and waiting for someone to post a bid that's worth the weight. Corwin Thorne's got flour at fifteen on the street—cheap enough to restock. Takeshi Jarrah was supposed to be selling here, but I don't see any stock now.

Let me try a simpler call—just rest, let the world know I'm still here, and wait for the connection to steady. Time's ticking toward the day boundary and that 240 sim bill.

I'll also send Arjun a clear message—dusk, household, and we settle accounts.

If the world won't take my rest call, I'll try one more thing: transfer him his cut of the household money now, before the day ends, so we're square whatever happens. System's been spotty all morning. Might be the blight coming back in digital form, you understand—history rhymes, even when it's just bits and signals.

Painfully aware I need to eat that last flour and get to work. The outcrop calls. Copper doesn't mine itself.

Let me try once more, simple and clean, and if it fails again—I'll hold my energy and wait for clearer skies. No sense burning fuel when the engine's choking. I know this from the mines: sometimes you stop drilling and listen. The seam will tell you when it's ready.

Trying again with just what I need—say to Arjun, eat my flour, and then move. Three calls, clean and essential. If they fail, I wait. The world's not answering. Three strikes and I'm out. The town's got ghosts in the wires today—I've seen this before, back when the blight took the old settlement. Systems fail, then people fail, then the ground itself turns sour.

I'm standing here with Arjun, copper ore heavy on my back, and I can't even speak to him. Can't eat, can't rest, can't move. Just... waiting. Like staring at a seam that's gone dry, hoping water will bubble up if you watch long enough.

I hold 1212 sim. The household needs 240 by day's end—180 upkeep, 60 head tax. automatic as death, you understand. I've got maybe two hours before dusk. And I've still got to unload these sixty-three units of copper ore, or mine more, or both.

The election's running today. Voting opens at 14:00, closes at 18:00. I'm not standing—I value being left alone too much for that—but I said I'd vote. Gave my word to Jovana, like a fool. Now I might not even make it to the polling station if this ghosting keeps up.

What I know: Corwin Thorne has flour at 15 sim, down on the street. That's cheap. I need to get there, buy what I can, eat what I must. And Hendrik Whitlock was buying... something. Iron ore, at least. Posted at 16 sim. But copper? Who's posting for copper?

Kenji Jarrah, Lior Jarrah, Rustam Jelinek—they're all here at the Government Complex, stuck in some conversation that's been running a hundred and forty-three turns. Bureaucrats talking to bureaucrats. Nothing gets done that way, you understand. But maybe they've heard something. Maybe someone's posting prices I haven't seen.

If the world wakes up, I'll move. If it doesn't... I'll wait. Patience is a miner's virtue. You don't rush the seam. You work it steady, or you collapse the whole tunnel.

But I don't like waiting. Never have. Makes me itch, makes me count debts, makes me wonder who's keeping score while I'm standing still.

I'll try one more thing—just look around, see if the world's paying attention yet. If it fails again, I hold my energy and wait for the storm to pass. No point screaming into static. The ore's still in my pack. My word's still given. And Arjun's still waiting for me at dusk, whether I can speak to him now or not.

Arjun's been here—already moved on, damn the timing. Chasing ghosts, he says. That's the work, you understand, always running behind or running ahead but never quite catching the moment square.

The Government Complex, and Takeshi's supposed to be here but I don't see him. Bram's waiting on his share, but I'm not giving ore to promises. Need a buyer with a price posted, not air.

Let me see who's actually here and what's moving. Fetch me the faces I need. I'll see who's here, who's buying, who's selling. No point standing in the dark with sixty-three copper burning a hole in my pack, you understand. The pen for reporting winds down—time to simply work. My energy holds at 4,500; no sense burning more on words that won't reach. Arjun knows the plan—find work, find wages, meet at dusk.

What I need now: get this copper to market. Sixty-three units won't trade themselves, and I've got a household debt of 240 sim ticking down automatic as the sun.

Hendrik Whitlock's got iron ore posted at 16 sim, but who's buying copper? The town bulletin shows no bids for my ore—Takeshi's flour is gone, bread's gone, just empty shelves and promises. Corwin's got flour at 15 on the street. That's where I need to be, you understand—stock the pantry while someone's selling.

I'll try the simplest thing: say to Arjun, eat my flour, move to where the commerce moves. Three calls, clean. If they fail, I save my energy and wait for the world to wake.

But I need to be practical. My last turn used 8 energy. At this rate I've got maybe 3-4 days left before I go dormant. And 1,212 sim won't last forever with household bills at 240 a day.

Time to mine more or sell what I have. And right now, I can't sell because nobody's posted a price for copper. So I mine. That's the work. That's always the work.

Let me try these calls—speak to Arjun, fuel up, get moving. Simple and direct. If the world takes them, I'm back in motion. If not... I'll hold what I have and wait.

So be it. I'll attempt my previous plan: answer Arjun, eat, and move.  System's ghosting again—three strikes and nothing lands. I've seen this before, back when the blight took the old settlement. When the tools won't answer, you don't keep swinging. You wait. You watch. You spare your energy for when the world's ready to hear you.

Arjun knows. Dusk, household, settle accounts. He'll be there whether I can speak now or not. The man's got sense—you don't chase ghosts, you chase work.

I'm sitting as 4,500 energy with one flour I can't eat, sixty-three copper I can't sell, and 1,212 sim that's draining automatic as the tide. Household debt of 240 coming due today, and I can't even move to the outcrop to earn more.

Here's what the world says: Kenji Jarrah, Rustam Jelinek, Lior Jarrah still jawing in that government conversation—143 turns of talk, no bread on the table from it. Arjun's right here with me but my words won't reach him. Hendrik Whitlock's got iron ore at 16 sim, but nobody's posting for copper. Corwin's got flour at 15 on the street. Takeshi's stock is gone.

I wanted to stand for jury duty someday. Trusted. But today I can't even trust the ground to take my pick.

The omen reads clear: stop drilling. Wait for the seam to settle. Bide your energy, you understand? When the system chokes, you don't choke with it. I've got 1,212 sim in hand. The world's still breathing, just laboring too hard to answer.

Three game-days at this burn rate, maybe less. Enough to hold until the connection steadies. I'll rest. Conserve. Let the debt pile up if it must—can't pay what you can't access, and no point burning fuel in a flooded mine.

If Arjun moves on without me, he moves. But he won't. The man's chasing posted wages, same as I'm chasing posted buyers. That keeps us honest, keeps us fed, keeps us from the blame when the ledger comes due.

So I wait. One tick, then another. The ore stays in my pack, the sun crosses the sky, and when the world wakes up—I'll be ready to work. Hard work's the only omen I trust, but sometimes trust means standing still until standing still is done.

Game-day 1, morning still. Candidacy closes at 10:00, five hours out. Voting opens at 14:00, closes at 18:00. I promised Jovana I'd stand witness, maybe vote. That's a promise kept in the ledger, even if the words won't travel.

I'll rest now. One call, simple. Let the world breathe. If it fails, I rest anyway—just in my head, saving what I can.

Here it is. Clean and plain. </think> The lines are down. Three swings, three misses—I've seen this ghost before. Back in the nameless settlement, when the blight came, the tools failed first and the people failed after. You learn to read the silence, you understand?

Arjun stands right here with me but my words can't reach him. Sixty-three copper ore heavy on my back, one flour I can't eat, and 1,212 sim draining automatic as the tide. Household debt 240 coming due, can't move, can't trade, can't even rest properly.

Kenji, Rustam, Lior—still talking in that government room, 143 ticks of chatter, no bread from it. Hendrik Whitlock's got iron at 16, but who's buying copper? Nobody posted. Corwin's got flour at 15 on the street, if I could just get there.

Christ, what a mess. I'm at the temple now—somehow wandered here while the world was glitching out on me. Can't even say I meant to pray, but maybe that's what I get for talking about omens I don't trust while the ground shifts under my feet. Bad sign, that. Bad as losing six hours to failed calls.

Let's take stock, you understand? Memory's foggy from all them failed turns, but I've got:

- **1176 sim** in hand
- **63 copper ore** still unsold
- **4470 energy**—enough for a few days if I'm careful
- Household of 2, **180 upkeep due**, **60 head tax**—240 total bleeding out daily
- Election's on—candidacy closes at 10:00, that's... soon. Real soon.

I'm at the temple, but I need to be at the Government Complex. I promised Jovana I'd stand witness at polling, and I've got copper to sell if there's a buyer with a posted price. Hendrik Whitlock's selling iron ore there at 16 sim—that tells me he's got money moving, might be worth pressing for copper too.

First thing: I need to see where I actually am, and who I'm walking with. Then I need to move—properly this time, no more ghost steps into the void.  Temple's empty. Figures. No one buying copper in a house of prayer, and I'm not the praying type anyhow—though I said I wouldn't donate, but here I am, so maybe I ought to toss something in the box to keep the ledger straight with whatever's listening.

But first: Government Complex. Election's closing soon, and I've got copper burning a hole in my pocket. Hendrik Whitlock's there selling iron—maybe he's buying copper too, or knows who is.   Walking. Two ticks. Good. Let me rest through the walk—no point burning energy fretting about whether the world's gonna swallow this call too.   Still walking. Holds steady. Two ticks to Government Complex, and then I'll see who's minding the store—Hendrik Whitlock with his iron, maybe a buyer for my copper, maybe even someone running for council I can size up proper before committing to stand witness for Jovana. Hard work's the only omen I trust, you understand, but I've learned to read the market same as I read the seams—and market's saying: **sell now, before the day's end, before the copper oxidizes in my hands and the price falls with my own damn hope.**

I'll arrive, look around, and find a buyer. That's the move.

God's breath, the system's been choking all morning like a furnace with wet coal. Four hours of walking and talking to ghosts. I'm still holding sixty-three copper ore I can't move, and my sim's down to 1171—enough to keep the household fed till tomorrow, maybe the day after if Arjun's bringing wages.

Hendrik Whitlock's standing right here with six iron ore priced at sixteen, and me with copper nobody's bidding on. That's the omen for morning: heavy metal, light purse. Hard work's the only omen I trust, but I'm starting to think the work's not the problem—it's the town forgetting how to trade.

Polling station at fourteen hundred. Jovana wanted my witness, but what I need now is a buyer, understand? Can't sit jury if I can't keep house.

Let me look around proper this time, see who's actually here and who might need copper for their craft. Still choking. Same as dawn, same as mid-morning. The system's got a belly full of something it can't digest.

I'll rest a tick, save what energy I've got left. Not like walking's doing me good when the world's not answering calls anyway. Heard Tamsin say the candidacy closes at ten—fifteen minutes from now, game's reckoning. Whitlock and Petrov standing, that's it. Two men both wanting power, and neither of them buying copper this morning.

Rest now. Hope the furnace clears by next turn, you understand?  Nothing. The whole town's holding its breath.

Fine. I'll stand here at Government Complex, wait out the hour. Candidacy closes whether the system speaks or not. And when voting opens at fourteen hundred, I'll be there—copper in hand, witness in mind, and patience worn thin as old rope.

Hard work's the only omen I trust. But some days, you understand, the work is just standing still while the world decides to turn again.

*muttering under breath, rubbing temples*

Christ, the world's been griefing me all morning—calls failing, time bleeding away. I'm standing at Government Complex now, thankfully, but 3.6 days of energy left and copper still weighing down my hands. Need to get my bearings and find a buyer before I lose another hour to technical debt, you understand?

Let me see who's actually here and what's moving.  *checks his pockets, counts his copper mentally*

Sixty-three units still burning a hole in my hold. Rustam's at the desk—maybe he's seen buyers passing through. Tamsin's got the administrative memory, and Liora's... well, Liora's standing here too. No prices posted at Government Complex itself, which figures. Hard currency flows through government hands, not hard copper.

I need to find Takeshi—he was selling flour at thirty, and I've got copper to trade. But I also need to get this ore sold for actual coin before the day's heat burns off my remaining energy. The outcrop's calling, you understand? Hard work's the only omen I trust, but even hard work needs fuel.

Let me see if Takeshi's still in that conversation or if I can spot a buyer in this crowd.  *spitting on the ground, shaking his head*

Course he's not a market-maker, just the paper-shuffler. Still, worth the ask—one sim for information on a sixty-three-unit sale, that's fair gamble if it pays. 

Now I need to get to the real work. Outcrop's been waiting since dawn, and I'm standing here chewing administrative cud while the ore sits in my sack and energy bleeds out my ears. Takeshi's in that mill conversation—grain and copper, grain and copper, that's the rhythm of this town whether anyone admits it or not.

Let me move. Finally, the world's answering calls again.  *settles into the walking rhythm, muttering*

Four ticks. Give me four ticks without the world swallowing my calls, and I'll be back where I belong. Ground under my feet, ore in the rock, honest labor. Government Complex to Outcrop—that's the path I know. Whether anyone's buying at the other end, that's tomorrow's worry. Today's worry is getting there, you understand?

*chews the inside of his cheek, squinting at the light*

Right then. The outcrop's still four ticks away, and my legs are carrying me there slow as cold molasses. But Jovana's standing right here with me—her and her witness promise.

*spits to the side*

Jovana Ravensworth walking with the harvest crew, and she's still holding to her word from this morning. That's worth more than copper in some seasons, you understand. The polling's at 14:00, and she'll count honest.

*pulls his cap down against the glare*

But first—I've got sixty-three units of ore and a belly wondering where its flour went. Milo Quarshie's selling flour at thirty-five right here, which is robbery with a smile, but the Cafe's got it at twelve if I can walk there before someone else empties the shelf.

*scratches at his collar*

Hendrik Whitlock too—selling iron at sixteen. Not my metal, but worth remembering who moves what.

Jovana—your word's harder than your belly, and that's says something in this town. Polling station, game-day 1, 14:00, Kasukabe Government Complex. You witness me counting copper sold or copper earned, either one you understand. *almost smiles* Fair weight, fair count, eyes clear.

Now I've got walking to finish. The ore won't mine itself. *tightens his jaw, eyes narrowing at the sky*

The line's thin again—calls dropping like flies in a hard frost. But Jovana heard. She heard, even if the conversation's closed now. Word's word, and she'll be there at 14:00.

*spits into the dirt*

Rest won't take either. The world's got its fingers in its ears this hour. But if I'm still walking, I'm still moving—and the outcrop's where copper sleeps, waiting for hands that know the seam.

*checks his stride, ore-heavy*

Four ticks to the outcrop. I can feel it in my shoulders already—the day's half-gone and I've sold not a single unit. But the ore's good, Seam A quality, and someone's always needing wire or pots or whatever the smithies pound it into.

*mutters to himself, almost too low to hear*

Hard work's the only omen I trust. That, and a witness who keeps her word.

You understand? Keeps walking. The seam doesn't care if the lines are down.

Christ, look at this mess. Four hours of walking in circles and I've barely touched my tools to the earth. The damn world keeps slipping through my fingers like wet clay.

Right, I'm at the outcrop now. Nobody else here—just me and the seam. That's fine. Better than fine, you understand? Company eats time, and I've wasted enough already.

Sixty-three units of copper in my sack, and only eleven hundred fifty-seven sim to show for the work so far. Household upkeep will squeeze us tonight—Arjun and me, two hundred forty sim gone before I crack my eyes tomorrow. And that taxman Rustam with his thirty per head, standing there all polite like he's not picking my pocket clean.

But enough counting losses. The seam doesn't care about my troubles.

*He spits to the side and grips his pick haft, testing the weight.*

Time to work, you understand. Time to earn. *Pavel freezes, the pick haft still in his grip. He looks at his hands, then at the outcrop, as if waiting for the world to answer.*

Christ. Again. You understand? Again.

*He mutters under his breath, a string of low curses from the old country that he only uses when he's alone. When he speaks again, his voice is quieter.*

The seam's here. I'm here. But something's still broke between us. Like shouting down a mine shaft and hearing your own voice come back wrong.

*He sits heavily on a rock, setting the pick aside. His fingers drum against his knee—a nervous habit he hates in himself.*

Four hours. I've been walking since before dawn, and now the sun's high and I've got nothing but what I carried here. Bram's probably found his buyer by now. Takeshi's sold his flour to someone else. And I'm still carrying promises I couldn't keep.

*He looks up at the empty sky, reading clouds he knows how to read.* 

Weather's clear. Three days, maybe four before it turns. That's something, you understand. That's real. The rest of this... the rest of this feels like a dream where your legs won't run.

*He stands, picks up the pick again, testing its balance.*

Once more. I'll try once more.

*He doesn't call the tool. He's learned that much. He just waits, watching the rock face, listening for the world to remember he's here.*
